hypothesis: The key is a weak/guessable constant (dictionary or TE words, raw/md5/sha1/sha256)
test: Decrypt the known filename block (IV@0x70, ct@0x300) and match plaintext 'firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip' across ~1.18M candidate keys
notes: No hit. Key is not a simple dictionary/TE-derived constant.

hypothesis: The same key is used across all firmware versions (only the IV changes)
test: Compare key-index byte and IV across all 7 files
notes: key index = 0xFF in every file; every IV differs. Consistent with one global key + random IV, but cannot be proven without the key.

hypothesis: The raw AES key is stored somewhere in the 0x00-0x400 header
test: Scan header for high-entropy 16/32-byte runs
notes: Only two non-trivial regions: IV (16B @0x70) and the encrypted filename blob (256B @0x300). No raw key.

hypothesis: The cipher is a padded block mode (CBC/ECB), not a stream mode (CTR/CFB/OFB)
test: Check whether ciphertext size == plaintext length + PKCS#7 padding
notes: All 7 files: (0x400 + len + PKCS#7-pad) == filesize exactly. Stream modes do not pad, so mode is CBC (or ECB).

hypothesis: ECB is used for the filename blob (would repeat identical zero-pad blocks)
test: Count repeated 16-byte blocks in the 0x300..0x3FF blob
notes: Zero repeats in all files -> not ECB-with-zero-pad; consistent with CBC.

hypothesis: The community primary source documents the scheme
test: Read archived Reddit thread be1nl6 + op-forums topic 7677
notes: Device is ADSP-BF703 (Blackfin); header/IV/length confirmed; plaintext is firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip. Poster never found the key.

hypothesis: A public decryption key or tool exists
test: GitHub repo/code search, Sourcegraph, Wayback, op-forums
notes: No published OP-Z .zfw key or decryptor found; only OP-1 (XTEA) tooling by TabascoEye, which needs a key too.

hypothesis: The BF703 hardware AES engine with OTP key slot (key index 0xFF) can decrypt the file without exposing the key
test: Load code on the BF703 via its debug port that runs the on-chip AES engine on the payload with the hidden key slot
notes: Requires hardware access. This is the recommended real path.

hypothesis: The key is a real human password
test: rockyou.txt (14.34M) x {raw16,raw32,md5,sha256} -> ~57M keys vs known filename block
notes: Full rockyou exhausted, no hit.

hypothesis: The key is derived from a file clue (IV, filename, version, ciphertext) via a KDF
test: PBKDF2/HKDF/repeated-SHA256, key=f(IV), f(filename), f(version), f(ciphertext), IV||IV
notes: No hit. IVs also not hashes of the version string.

hypothesis: The key is stored somewhere in the file
test: Scan every aligned 16- and 32-byte window of the whole file as an AES key
notes: No hit; header really only holds IV + encrypted filename.

hypothesis: The whole file is XOR/stream encrypted (known plaintext leaks keystream)
test: keystream = C xor P; test periods 1-32; pairwise XOR structuredness of payloads
notes: No periodicity; all pairwise XORs are random (zeros ~ n/256). Not ECB, no reused nonce.

hypothesis: A padding oracle over the OP-Z upgrade serial console decrypts the firmware without the key
test: Read rez wiki (billymeter) confirming the CBC padding oracle + unencrypted-zip bypass
notes: Software-only route exists but returns plaintext, not the key, and needs the device.

hypothesis: The literal 256-bit AES key can be recovered from the .zfw files alone
test: All of the above
notes: Key is in BF703 OTP (cf. OP-1 OTP page 0xd0). Not in or derivable from the file.

hypothesis: Some version-pair comparison leaks the key or plaintext (shared plaintext across versions)
test: All 21 pairs: aligned + unaligned shared 16-byte ciphertext windows + common prefixes
notes: 0 shared 16-byte windows in every pair. CBC with distinct IVs leaks nothing across versions.

hypothesis: The encrypted payload is really an extractable zip/contains a plaintext header
test: Check payload for PK/zip structure and any low-entropy region
notes: Payload is uniformly high entropy; zip only exists after decryption.

hypothesis: The upgrade serial console can be turned into a full decryption oracle for the payload
test: Realise console prints AES_dec(blob)^IV; place payload blocks in 0x300, set IV@0x70 to preceding block
notes: CBC chaining inside the 256B blob -> 256 bytes of payload plaintext per query. Implemented + self-tested in oracle_decrypt.py.

hypothesis: The AES key is published somewhere on the internet
test: GitHub/Sourcegraph/Wayback/Reddit archives/op-forums/lines/search engines, wiki git history
notes: Community (rez wiki, 2019-2021) never recovered the key; nothing published.

hypothesis: The upgrade serial console prints the decrypted 0x300 blob (usable as an oracle)
test: Connect real unit, drop a .zfw, eject, capture the CDC console
notes: bootdisk: prints 'filename found: firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip'; on a crafted blob it printed our injected bytes.

hypothesis: Payload ciphertext placed in the 0x300 slot is decrypted to payload plaintext
test: Craft blob=payload blocks, IV=0x70 IV, eject, capture
notes: Printed junk; XOR with IV and original 0x3F0 block = 'PK\x03\x04\x14\x00...' = valid ZIP header.

hypothesis: The payload has its own IV (IV@0x70)
test: Compare printed block vs known payload block 0
notes: Payload chains from the LAST filename-blob block at 0x3F0. One continuous CBC stream from 0x300.

hypothesis: After eject the device reboots and needs SCREEN+power to return
test: Check serial + LUN + diskutil after a failed read
notes: Device STAYS in upgrade mode (serial alive); only the mass-storage LUN disappears. Failed read does not reboot.

hypothesis: A failed read leaves the drive remounted so we can loop cheaply
test: Wait 15s after eject and check /Volumes/OP-Z
notes: LUN does not come back on its own; a cheap re-export (USB re-enumerate) is the open question.

hypothesis: The console print is length-delimited (full 256 bytes raw)
test: Inspect raw bytes of the printed blob
notes: It is a C string: stops at the first 0x00, so binary windows get truncated.

hypothesis: The upgrade-mode CDC console accepts commands (is bidirectional)
test: Send C0 routing=0x01 type len_be32 payload frames to /dev/cu.usbmodemX3CJN79E1
notes: 0x00->pong, 0x02->version, 0x07->metadata, 0x35->component versions + chip_id, 0x2b->yaffs stats. Reply routing is 0x1e.

hypothesis: The console command type space is safe to enumerate
test: Send every type 0x00-0x7f with an empty payload
notes: Type 0x15 IS a NAND format action (re-runs with a fresh timestamp each call). Probing it cost the normal-boot path.

hypothesis: Type 0x15 on the upgrade console is destructive to the internal NAND/boot state
test: Observe logs when 0x15 is sent, then power-cycle and check boot mode
notes: Logs 'nand: formatting 4096 nand blocks..'; afterwards the unit ONLY boots to update mode and the user filesystem is empty/rebuilt.

hypothesis: The normal-boot path can be restored by reflashing firmware
test: Reflash 1.2.45 and 1.1.12; factory reset (SCREEN+STOP); power-drain; USB re-enumerate; power-on with no USB
notes: All fail. Flashing logs 'os: OK (0)' / 'already upgraded to 1.2.45' yet the unit still returns in update mode: the destroyed state lies outside the four .zfw components.

hypothesis: The stuck update-mode state is a stuck SCREEN button line
test: Power on holding PROJECT; power on with USB unplugged; TRACK still selects content mode
notes: OS boots in content mode and the button is mechanically fine; plain, PROJECT and no-USB power-ons all give update mode.

hypothesis: The $62 text command (debug-crash / disable-debug) can clear the stuck state
test: Send $62 SysEx over USB MIDI
notes: Unreachable: the OP-Z exposes no MIDI endpoint outside playable mode, and the upgrade console ignores text payloads (0x00 just echoes them).

hypothesis: Recovery is possible from the running OS via content mode
test: Check content mode for a serial console, MIDI endpoint, or crash-report file in the filesystem root
notes: No USB CDC/MIDI endpoint was found, but content imports do work. Decompiling the 1.3.0 app shows Content::importExistingFile only overwrites files whose internal destination already exists (userPresets.dat excepted), so new internal files cannot be created this way; syncImportFolder can also DELETE internal config files.

hypothesis: The official app contains filesystem defaults and a native simulator useful for identifying the crashing initialization path
test: Locate the official app resources and inspect the defaults and general-config consumer without executing device commands
notes: APK assets/factory-plug-cache gives the full factory plug table: 35 plugs, 58 presets with 18-byte values, 16 engines with memoryslot; extracted to opz-factory-plugs.json. libSnakePlugin.so supplies decompiled loadSettings/LoadDMXConfig/Content/PlugManager.

hypothesis: The device boot crash is caused by the missing /yaffs2/user/settings/ directory (or by general.json content)
test: Compare the device crash log against the decompiled app SnakeSystem::loadSettings and LoadDMXConfig
notes: Both functions log a distinct message before every early return and cannot deref NULL; the device log contains none of those messages. The crash is downstream of the general-config parse, in saveSettings/SynthInit/sequencerInit (plug+engine table init).

hypothesis: The updater content-copy stage can restore filesystem files without flashing custom code
test: Inspect archive layout and content-copy rules before constructing any recovery archive
notes: Captured genuine upgrade logs copying 18 files with content: OK, so a reflash does copy content, but /yaffs2/user/settings/ is still missing afterwards. Archive layout never inspected because the plaintext zip cannot be captured.

hypothesis: Content-mode userPresets.dat import can create or populate the internal settings directory
test: Verify documented mapping and import implementation before using a known-good preset file
notes: App source: config/userPresets.dat is the one file importExistingFile will CREATE (the strstr check short-circuits the destination-exists guard). It maps to config/userPresets.dat in the user tree, not to settings/ - a genuine write path, but not a settings/ writer.

hypothesis: The bootloader writes the decrypted plaintext firmware zip to the update volume as a file the host can read
test: Poll /Volumes/OP-Z every 150 ms during a PLAY-triggered and an eject-triggered upgrade, with a diskutil re-mount hammer
notes: The console lists firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip in the FAT, but PLAY re-enumerates the whole USB device and eject only returns the volume after the upgrade with a regenerated FAT. No host-visible window; the plaintext firmware stays out of reach by this route.

hypothesis: A wipe-then-install (0x15 format, then immediately flash 1.2.45) restores the normal-boot path
test: Stage the genuine .zfw on the update volume, verify, send 0x15, verify the file, eject to flash
notes: The format destroys the staged .zfw (the update volume is backed by the same NAND) so no install happens; the bootloader loops 'bootdisk: upgrade was unsuccessful, system won't reset.' and the volume never returns writable.

hypothesis: The official engine binaries (engines/<name>.engine) can be obtained from the internet
test: Fetch the app DLC catalogue and engine assets without authentication
notes:
GET /_api/id/products/597caf1a-.../dlcs is public (200, 91 KB); GET /_api/id/my/products/

/assets/ returns application/octet-stream with no auth. All 21 engines downloaded to engines/ (~103 kB).

hypothesis: The unit crashes because engines for plug ids 10/13/14/17/43 are missing
test: Stage all 21 engines as engines/*.engine, fill the ~NN.engine ghost slots and samplepacks/user/<id>.engine, then eject and read the crash log
notes: The crash is unchanged (RETX 0x80117baa) and no 'importing' lines were logged, but it is NOT yet confirmed whether the engines landed internally - the content disk did not show engines/ before this pass, so an install failure and a non-causal engine are not distinguished. Re-check on the next content-mode boot.

hypothesis: The content disk can create new internal files
test: Compile a valid userPresets.dat and upload it to config/
notes: userPresets.dat imports SUCCESS and creates the directory (createFolderRecursive), but it is the single exception; general.json/dmx.json were skipped and quarantined into rejected/config/.

hypothesis: The missing config/general.json causes the boot crash
test: Compare crash logs with general.json present, absent, and device-regenerated
notes: Same RETX 0x80117baa with the file present (22:49), absent (23:28), and present+loading (23:33). The fault is after loadSettings.

hypothesis: Files the device cannot import are silently skipped
test: Check the content disk after uploading config/general.json and config/dmx.json
notes: Both were moved to rejected/config/ on the content disk - the device quarantines rejected imports rather than dropping them.

hypothesis: A reflash can restore the user-tree contents (settings/, engines/, samples)
test: Flash 1.2.45 repeatedly and inspect the content disk and crash log
notes: After three flashes settings/ and engines/ are still absent and all 28 files under samplepacks/ are 0 bytes.

hypothesis: A host can install engine binaries into /yaffs2/user/engines/ via the content disk
test: Stage engines/*.engine, fill the ~NN.engine ghost slots and samplepacks/user/<id>.engine, eject, then re-check the content disk
notes: Every staged file was deleted: no engines/ dir, ghost slots back to only ~13.engine, samplepacks/user/ gone. The last import logged no importing lines. The content disk is a four-folder interface (config/projects/bounces/rejected); samplepacks/ is a read-only re-export of the internal tree.

hypothesis: BLE-MIDI can reach the file transport while the unit is in content mode
test: Scan for BLE-MIDI advertising in content mode
notes: Untested. Structurally unlikely: content mode skips both the general-config load and the plug/engine init, so SynthInit/MidiInit never run - which is exactly why content mode does not crash.

hypothesis: general.json is derived from something (slot config, settings, a template) and we are supplying it wrongly
test: Decompile SnakeSystem::saveSettings and loadSettings
notes: saveSettings writes exactly ten global booleans read from the same file; it depends on nothing else. {} yields a valid file; the device regenerated its own identical 336-byte copy.

hypothesis: The boot crash is in SnakeSystem::saveSettings / the general-config write
test: Read saveSettings and writeJsonFile
notes: saveSettings is a pure bool -> JSON conversion with no pointer dereference; writeJsonFile only reports failure. The device demonstrably wrote general.json successfully at 23:33.

hypothesis: The missing settings/slotConfiguration.json makes the device use hard-coded defaults whose engines are absent, and that is the null dereference
test: Decompile PlugManager::_importSlotConfiguration and Content::engineFileExists, then supply the engines
notes: The default map is 13,14,15,17,21,25,28,31,34,36,37,39,60,70,80,100 (exactly the ~NN.engine ghosts). engineFileExists(id) tests <id>.engine in the samplepacks scan, and we have engines for 13,14,17,25,31,34,39. Staging 101 <id>.engine files under samplepacks/user/ produced no import and an identical crash - but samplepacks/ behaves as export-only, so this is unresolved, not disproved.

hypothesis: A host can install engines by writing <id>.engine into samplepacks/user/
test: Stage 101 files across three layouts, eject, then re-check survival on the next content-mode boot
notes: samplepacks/user/ is gone entirely (0 files) while config/ and rejected/ are intact. samplepacks/ is export-only: host-written files are discarded. The engine hypothesis is out of host reach, not disproved.

hypothesis: The boot crash is caused by the internal plug/engine tables being absent after the 0x15 format
test: Decompile _importSlotConfiguration, _importPlugDefinitions, loadSettings, saveSettings, Synth::init and the crash logs
notes: With settings/slotConfiguration.json gone the OS installs its hard-coded default 16-slot map (13,14,15,17,21,25,28,31,34,36,37,39,60,70,80,100) but only five plugs exist (10,14,17,43,13) and settings/plugs.json is ENOENT. The null read happens in the plug/engine binding: RETX 0x80117baa, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x0, and no dmx log line, so it is before DmxController::init.

hypothesis: config/userPresets.dat maps to internal settings/plugPresets.dat and its import creates /yaffs2/user/settings/
test: Compare the ENOENT after plugmanager: save slot configuration across the 22:49/23:23/23:28 vs 23:33/23:38 logs
notes: ENOENT present in all logs before the import and absent in all logs after it, with the flash attempts in between failing to change it. copyFile runs createFolderRecursive on the destination, creating settings/.

hypothesis: A targeted upgrade-console probe can find a read/flash-access command to recover the OS image
test: Vary the payload of the tiny read commands 0x39/0x1a with addresses, then probe only types adjacent to known read-only commands with a liveness PING after each
notes: 0x39 ignores its payload entirely (returns a monotonic clock rising 1-2 per command) and 0x1a is one-shot. Types 0x2c/0x2a/0x38/0x3b/0x1b all return nothing; console and version string unchanged before/after. The console is identity/telemetry only: no file-read, memory-read or block-read command.

hypothesis: The console command space contains more usable commands than the ones already known
test: Probe 0x2c, 0x2a, 0x38, 0x3b, 0x1b adjacent to known read-only commands, empty payload, liveness check after each
notes: All five returned nothing. The complete answering set is 0x00, 0x02, 0x07, 0x15 (destructive), 0x1a (one-shot), 0x2b (one-shot), 0x35, 0x39.

hypothesis: 0x39 is a memory-read primitive taking an address
test: Send 0x39 with 4-byte big- and little-endian address payloads and compare replies
notes: The payload has no effect; the value increments 1-2 per command (6ac6d9e0, e1, e3, e5, ...). It is a monotonic clock / epoch timestamp.

hypothesis: SER_MSG_BF_ENTER_DFU (0x29) can put the Blackfin into DFU for host memory access
test: Send 0x29 over the upgrade console; resolve the enum value from the APK metadata
notes: The enum value is confirmed 0x29, but it is an app->OS message handled by SnakeSystem, not by the bootloader, so update mode ignores it (empty reply). In normal mode the OS crashes before MidiInit, so the app cannot send it either.

hypothesis: The bootloader console exposes NAND read/write commands alongside 0x15 (format)
test: Probe the NAND-family neighbourhood 0x16,0x17,0x14,0x13,0x18,0x19 with a canary file, volume check, port check, ping and version check after each send
notes: All six returned nothing and every damage detector stayed clean. 0x15 is the ONLY NAND operation reachable from the console - there is no read, write, erase or verify command. The flashing machinery is internal to the upgrade path, not console-addressable.

hypothesis: The updater accepts an unencrypted zip instead of an encrypted .zfw
test: Place a plain zip named firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip in the volume root and trigger with eject, capturing the console
notes: No decryption attempted; console shows [extract] progress 85/85 then upgrade started, i.e. the plain zip was accepted and extracted by the updater. This is a host-controlled data path into the updater.

hypothesis: A crafted zip can carry a content component that restores /yaffs2/user/{settings,engines} and repairs the unit
test: Satisfy the updater component checks and include the missing internal files in the content component
notes: The updater aborted on the first gate: failed to find ble firmware file -> upgrade not compatible with this device. Component names, the version/already-installed check and the content layout are still unknown. Risk: dummy os/bootloader payloads could be written to flash and a bad bootloader write is terminal.

hypothesis: A plain zip in the volume root gives a host write primitive into the internal filesystem
test: Stage firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip with entries ../user/... and eject, then boot normally and read the crash log
notes: The updater builds each path as /yaffs2/upgrade/ + entry name and resolves .. unsanitised (disk_io error text shows /yaffs2/upgrade/../../P2.txt verbatim). One .. escapes to /yaffs2/; two abort the extraction. A 0-byte ../user/settings/slotConfiguration.json was read by the OS on the next boot, which logged plugmanager: failed to load slot configuration, loading defaults - a line that does not appear while that file is readable. Flat writes also persisted across a power cycle. /yaffs2/user/settings/ and /yaffs2/user/engines/ are now host-writable.

hypothesis: The boot crash is caused by the missing engine binaries for the DLC plugs
test: Install the 21 genuine DLC engine binaries at /yaffs2/user/engines/ via the plain-zip updater primitive, then boot normally and compare the crash
notes: The crash after installing the engines is byte-identical: same iid 0x00130026, same ADI_EXC_DATA_CPLB_MISS, same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, same RETX 0x80117baa and the same 7-frame callstack. Installing the engine files alone does not change the boot, so the leading root-cause candidate is dead. (Whether settings/plugs.json binds them into memory slots is still untested.)

hypothesis: The slot-to-plug map (settings/slotConfiguration.json) causes the boot crash
test: Replace slotConfiguration.json with a 0-byte file so the OS takes its readFile<=0 branch and falls back to the hard-coded default 16-slot map, then compare the crash
notes: The fallback branch was confirmed live (plugmanager: failed to load slot configuration, loading defaults) and the crash was unchanged: same RETX 0x80117baa and callstack. The valid-file, missing-file and 0-byte-file cases all crash identically, so the slot configuration is not the trigger.

hypothesis: The bootloader console exposes a NAND read/write family around the 0x15 format command
test: Probe 0x16,0x17,0x14,0x13,0x18,0x19 one at a time with empty payloads, checking a canary file, volume, serial port, ping and version after every send
notes: All six types returned nothing and all five damage detectors stayed clean. 0x15 is the only NAND operation reachable from the console - no read, no write, no erase, no verify.

hypothesis: The slot configuration content (which plug each track references) triggers the boot crash
test: Write a slotConfiguration.json in the device's own export schema with all 16 tracks referencing only plug id 10 (proven defined by the boot log), via the plain-zip write primitive, then boot normally and compare
notes: The next boot accepted the file cleanly - 0 occurrences of failed to load slot configuration and 0 of Invalid slot config json, so no fallback and no parse error - and then crashed identically: same iid 0x00130026, same RETX 0x80117baa, same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000 and the same callstack ending 0x08003e0c, 0x080234e8, 0x75657551. The content of the slot-to-plug map is not the trigger.

hypothesis: A plug id with no plug definition causes a NULL plug pointer dereference at boot
test: Decompile findOrCreatePlug and getPlugFromSlot in the app binary and check the lookup contract
notes: findOrCreatePlug cannot return NULL: it scans the 200 records of 0x7ac bytes and returns the index of the first record whose id field is zero, setting a flag if all 200 are used. An undefined id therefore yields an empty record, not a null pointer. This removes the most obvious null-deref candidate for the invariant DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000.

hypothesis: InstrumentManager::init or FxManager::init is the fault site
test: Decompile both from the app binary
notes: Both are literally return; in this build (Synth::init is just those two calls plus about 64 0x7fffffff sentinel writes), so SynthInit cannot be where the boot dies.

hypothesis: initArpeggio() is the fault site, because it is the only reader of the wiped user tree inside the fault window
test: Write the six arpeggiators/NN.txt files (format string %s/arpeggiators/%02d.txt confirmed in the app binary) and compare the crash
notes: Decompilation shows initArpeggio runs first in Sequencer::init, inside the bracket after load general config and before load dmx config; it reads the wiped /yaffs2/user/arpeggiators/ directory and on readFile<1 falls back via __strcpy_chk(v5, *(char**)(v3+i*8), 0x200) to a built-in string table before parseCode(). A null or absent entry in that table would fault at exactly address 0. Untested: the file content is a code language parsed by parseCode and its only known source is the app table at dat_1d5318, not yet extracted.

hypothesis: The missing plug definitions (settings/plugs.json / plugs.dat) are the boot-crash trigger
test: Write a complete settings/plugs.json in the device export schema (40 plugs, 21 engines, engine paths matching the installed binaries) via the write primitive, then boot normally
notes: The payload demonstrably took effect - the five found plug to import lines that appear in every previous boot dropped to zero, proving _importPlugDefinitions parsed the JSON and filled g_plugs - and the crash was byte-identical: same iid 0x00130026, same RETX 0x80117baa, same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, same 7-frame callstack. Also established that loadPlugDefinitions (banner load plug definitions) never runs in the normal boot path, so plugs.json is the only filler of that table.

hypothesis: The missing arpeggiator files drive the crash through initArpeggio / parseCode
test: Write all six arpeggiators/00.txt..05.txt with the byte-exact built-in patterns extracted from the app testPattern table, then boot normally
notes: The six files were written and extraction was clean, and the crash was byte-identical. Note the app has a working fallback (__strcpy_chk from testPattern[i]) for a failed read, so a missing or 0-byte arpeggiator file was already the safe path.

hypothesis: The crash depends on inputs to the normal-mode init sequence
test: Eliminate by live ablation every user-tree file that can be supplied from the host, then compare the crash each time
notes: Across two live ablation rounds the crash is invariant: engine binaries installed at /yaffs2/user/engines/, slotConfiguration.json valid and referencing only a defined plug, config/general.json 0-byte and regenerated, a complete plugs.json (applied, proven by the plug-import lines disappearing), and the six arpeggiator files. Same iid, same RETX 0x80117baa, same callstack every time. Since content mode runs the same OS successfully while skipping loadSettings/SynthInit/sequencerInit/MidiInit, the fault is specific to the normal-mode init sequence but not to any of these five inputs.

hypothesis: The app build is a faithful guide to the device build
test: Check the branch guarded by g_opzSim and the functions in the fault window
notes: g_opzSim resolves to 1 in the app (simulator) and 0 on the device, so Sequencer::init takes the other branch of the version call (0.1.0 vs 0.1.scr); InstrumentManager::init, FxManager::init and initHumanize are literally empty in the app and may do real work on the device. The app is reliable for schemas, path constants, symbol sizes and control flow, but not for branch-level behaviour.

hypothesis: The decrypted firmware archive can be captured off the volume in plaintext
test: Truncate a genuine .zfw so the bootloader decrypts and writes the archive but the upgrade fails, then read the volume
notes: Truncation works exactly as hoped - the archive IS written (the mass_storage scan finds firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip) - but the bootloader deletes processed firmware files before the volume can be mounted, and the archive is gone when the volume returns. The decrypt field layout was fully recovered from the plaintext log.

hypothesis: The boot crash is caused by a bad OS image
test: Feed the full genuine 1.2.45 archive and let the upgrade complete, then boot normally and compare
notes: The upgrade ran completely (content: OK, os: OK, the rest already installed) and the next boot still crashed identically: same iid 0x00130026, same RETX 0x80117baa, same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000. The OS image is genuine and current, so it is not the fault.

hypothesis: Every firmware component has now been restored, so the crash must be caused by something else
test: Reinstall the genuine firmware components and rebuild the user tree by hand, then compare the crash
notes: content and os were rewritten by the full 1.2.45 upgrade, bootloader and keyboard were rewritten by the 22:49 reflash, ble reports its correct version so the updater skips it, and the user tree was rebuilt via the write primitive - and the normal-mode boot faults at the same instruction every time. The fault is neither in a firmware component nor in any user-tree file reachable from the host.

hypothesis: A repair payload written through the plain-zip write primitive survives a firmware upgrade
test: Compare the found plug to import record indices before and after the genuine upgrade
notes: Before: indices 0,1,2,3,4. After: 0,3,4,12,2. The content component (18 files) rewrites the user tree, so host-installed /yaffs2/user/ files are transient across an upgrade and a repair must be re-applied afterwards.

hypothesis: Forcing a full rewrite of every firmware component fixes the boot
test: Downgrade to the genuine 1.1.12 archive to defeat the already-installed check, then reflash the genuine 1.2.45 archive, then compare the post-upgrade boot
notes: Both upgrades completed and wrote every component: content, os, bootloader (to alternating A/B slots - index 1 then index 0) and the PSoC keyboard, with ble correctly reported as already installed because its image is identical across all seven archives. The post-rewrite 1.2.45 boot still crashed identically: same iid 0x00130026, same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, same RETX 0x80117baa. The fault is not a firmware-image problem.

hypothesis: The bootloader has a single slot, so a bad bootloader write is unrecoverable
test: Watch the bootloader component progress line across two consecutive upgrades
notes: The log shows wrote bootloader to index 1 during the 1.1.12 downgrade and wrote bootloader to index 0 during the 1.2.45 reflash, i.e. two A/B slots with the flasher alternating between them. A bad bootloader write is recoverable through the other slot.

hypothesis: The keyboard component is flashed by the bootloader
test: Read the component results and console during a full upgrade
notes: After bootloader: OK and ble: Already installed the console shows main: Wake Leds followed by upgrade: psoc upgrade row 25 through 511 - the keyboard is a PSoC and its firmware is written row by row by the OS after it has started, not by the bootloader.

hypothesis: The update-mode bootloader implements SER_MSG_ENABLE_FACTORY_MODE_REQUEST (0x09) and needs the 0xF0 magic byte
test: Send 0x09 with payload F0 and F0000000 on the console with a canary and liveness checks around it
notes: Both variants returned nothing while PING still answered PONG and the version string was byte-identical, and the canary and volume were untouched. 0x09 is an OS-side message like BF_ENTER_DFU 0x29, and the OS serial handler comes up at MidiInit which is after the fault point, so factory mode is unreachable from the update-mode console.

hypothesis: The encrypted firmware can be decoded from the host without the AES key
test: Map the .zfw header, then slide a chosen-ciphertext window into the bootloader decrypted-filename oracle and read the printed plaintext
notes: The header is key index at 0x004, IV at 0x070, length u32 at 0x080 and a 256-byte encrypted filename field at 0x300, with the archive at 0x400. Placing the archive ciphertext from offset X in the name field and setting the IV to the block at X-16 makes the bootloader print the archive plaintext at X. Sliding to 0x400 returned a valid zip local header: 50 4b 03 04 ... which is PK\\x03\\x04. One crafted file yields 256 bytes of decrypted archive at any offset, with no key, and the read aborts without any flash write.

hypothesis: A host-side USB action can restore the mass-storage volume after an aborted read without a power cycle
test: Trigger a read, then try diskutil unmount, console session messages, dfu-util and libusb_reset_device, checking for a disk node after each
notes: In the post-abort state the device enumerates as OP_Z Boot (2367:000c) with no interfaces but a live CDC console. Waiting 105 s and ~25 min, GREETING 0x0b, POWER_MODE 0x06, POWER_ACTIVE 0x10, ACK 0x80, dfu-util -l (not a DFU device) and libusb_reset_device (which returns OK) all leave the volume absent; only a power cycle restores it. diskutil unmount does not even trigger the read and its LUN re-mounts instantly.

hypothesis: The zip central directory at the tail of the archive can be decoded in ~10-20 queries
test: Decode the last few KB of the payload with the sliding-window oracle and parse the central directory
notes: A zip central directory sits at the end of the file, so the tail yields every entry name, offset and size. The oracle yields 256 bytes per crafted file; each read costs one power cycle. Pending the user power cycling through the first batch. || SUPERSEDED 2026-10-10: the tail windows that suggested no directory were read at idx 1490063 and 1490319, both ==15 mod 16, i.e. misaligned, so the leak was pseudorandom (see new row on alignment). hypothesis: An unprivileged host action can re-insert the OP-Z update medium after a read

hypothesis: Masking the IV by 0x01 raises the oracle's yield per query
test: Measure the leak distribution on high-entropy data with and without first-block masking
notes: CBC makes the first block's plaintext D(C0) XOR IV; XORing the IV by 0x01 shifts it so a NUL in the first 16 bytes prints as 0x01. Measured mean leak 44 -> 161.7 bytes/probe; at N=200 that is ~31.6 KB/cycle, i.e. ~46 cycles for the full 1.49 MB payload instead of ~169.

hypothesis: Malformed console input can fault the bootloader into a watchdog reset

hypothesis: USB Bulk-Only class requests can restore the update medium unprivileged

hypothesis: A CDC break or DTR toggle resets the OP-Z and restores the medium

hypothesis: Some console routing target other than 0x01 carries a reset or medium-restore command
test: Sweep 76 routing values (0x00-0x3F plus 0x40-0xF0 step 0x10) with a PING frame each, fresh handle, 2 s medium watch, liveness checks and a final 60 s watch
notes: No routing value other than 0x01 replies, none disturbs the console, none restores the medium; console alive afterwards. hypothesis: A decrypted copy of the firmware exists somewhere on this machine

hypothesis: One of the remaining USB standard requests or CDC SET_LINE_CODING resets the device

hypothesis: The engine blobs share a decodable container header
test: Read the first 16 bytes of all 21 engines and test the fields against file sizes
notes: All 21 have 00 50 at 0x00, 0x11a00000 at 0x04, and payload size = filesize-16 at 0x0c (exact for every file, e.g. 6568-16=6552=0x1998). A TE Blackfin module is a 16-byte header (entry + base address + length) followed by the payload.

hypothesis: The crash callstack involves engine/plug code rather than only OS code
test: Compare the stable callstack frames from the crash log against the base address declared in the engine headers
notes: Frames 2 and 3 of the stable prefix are 0x11a03838 and 0x11a02586, both inside 0x11a0xxxx, the base address every engine header declares (0x11a00000); frame 1 (0x8002c438) is in the OS range. So the fault path passes through engine/plug code.

hypothesis: The crash frames are inside one specific engine
test: Compare the crash callstack frames against the base address declared identically by all 21 engines
notes: 0x11a00000 is declared by all 21 engines, so it cannot be a per-engine load address; it is a shared region. Frames 2 and 3 (0x11a03838, 0x11a02586) are +0x3838 and +0x2586 into that shared region, i.e. shared plugin-framework code, not a single engine.

hypothesis: The engine payloads are compressed or encoded
test: Measure entropy, printability and byte distribution across all 21 engine bodies (file minus the 16-byte header)
notes: Mean entropy 6.389 (8.0 = random), 25.8% printable, 18.8% zeros, top bytes 00/04/20/31/82/18/02 -> plain Blackfin code and data. A catalogue parameter-name search inside the bodies found nothing, consistent with those names living in the metadata. So the decrypted OS image will be raw analysable code needing no decompression.

hypothesis: The per-engine 16-bit field in the blob header identifies the engine (a name hash)
test: Compare 0xADxx against crc16 ccitt/xmodem/ibm/arc, crc32 low half and a 16-bit sum of each engine name in four case/extension variants
notes: 0/21 matches for every hash variant. The field is not correlated with file size or memoryslot either, and chord/cluster share the same value, so it is not a unique engine id. It is most plausibly the 16-bit operand of the 0x5000 opcode at offset 0-1.

hypothesis: The blob header fields needed for the decode are fully determined
test: Verify the payload offset and the size field across all 21 engines and check what remains unknown
notes: Header length 16 and payload size = filesize-16 hold EXACTLY for all 21 engines; offset 4-7 is the constant shared region 0x11a00000; offset 8-11 reserved. Only the per-engine 16-bit operand at offset 2-3 remains unexplained, and it is not needed to locate code inside a blob.

hypothesis: The shared region 0x11a00000 can be named from the app binary
test: Search libSnakePlugin.so for the constant as a u32, map the hit offsets to VAs and resolve ELF symbols
notes: The constant appears twice (file offsets 0x6932e, 0x6c5aa), confirming it is a real referenced address in the shared codebase, but both sit before .text (0xbf290) with no covering symbol, so the region cannot be named from the app. Identifying it needs the device image.

hypothesis: The app contains a Blackfin emulator or ISA reference usable to disassemble the firmware
test: Search the app's native libraries and metadata for Blackfin/ADSP/ISA keywords and for opcode-dispatch tables
notes: No Blackfin/ADSP strings in libSnakePlugin.so; the only 'blackfin' hit in global-metadata.dat is the SER_BLACKFIN console enum identifier, and 'opcode' hits are libunwind/DWARF strings. hypothesis: The .zfw AES key is present as a literal in a local host artifact

notes: 73,831,200 candidate keys, 0 hits in 1,060 s. The key is not a literal on the host, not a substring of any TE binary and not a hash of any string in them, so it exists only inside the device bootloader and no offline computation can decrypt a .zfw.

hypothesis: The AES-256 key can be recovered by exhaustive ASCII search
test: Measure the per-candidate cost (one AES block) and extrapolate the printable-ASCII keyspace at the measured rate

Optimisation buys log(X)/log(95) characters: 2x = +0.15 chars, 1e6x = +3 chars. Reachable frontier is exhaustive printable ASCII to 7 chars (4.3 days on this Mac); 8 chars = 1.1 years here or 7.7 days on a GPU rig; 10 chars is out of reach of any machine. Full key space 2^256 = 3.7e59 years at 1e10/s, and known plaintext gives no shortcut against AES-256.

test: Dump the SPI flash with a clip and search for 16/32-byte key material and boot state

hypothesis: A successful upgrade reboots the device and the medium returns without user action
test: Stage the genuine 1.2.45 archive, eject, capture the console, then wait for the volume and stage a second probe
notes: Cycle 1 (2026-10-10 18:45): console showed 'bootdisk: detected encrypted file', 31 extract steps, 3 'Already installed' lines and 'upgrade: [2026-10-10 17:45] successfully upgraded to 1.2.45'; the volume was available again by 18:46:20 and cycle 2 staged a fresh probe with no power cycle. hypothesis: A probe can leak a window AND keep the archive valid so the upgrade still succeeds
test: Craft a probe whose name field leaks payload blocks in the free name blocks (1, 2 and 15 kept genuine) and check whether the console reports 'successfully upgraded' as well as a leak
notes: Built and verified (name blocks 1,2,15 byte-identical to genuine), then run: the name check PASSED and the device decrypted the whole 1491600 bytes ('bootdisk: filename found: <binary>...r.zip' then 'decrypt .../1491600'), but it never wrote the payload ('mass_storage: comparing z_firmware_probe_000.zfw with firmware' and no extract at all), so no upgrade and no reboot. Two independent reasons: (1) the decrypted name IS the FAT filename, and the leaked bytes contain values below 0x20 (0e 4c 2c ef 05 05 ...), which FAT forbids, so the write fails and the update flow never starts; (2) the printed/used name is truncated at the genuine 37-byte length, so the free name blocks 3-14 are never printed at all - the best case on a valid-name path is ~32 bytes, not ~208. Leak and reboot are mutually exclusive: an autonomous leak loop is impossible, see FIRMWARE_ANALYSIS.md 65.6.

hypothesis: The device can read several staged probes per boot if the FAT directory stays readable

hypothesis: Crafted oracle windows reproduce the payload plaintext at any requested offset
test: Extract opzfarm.py:craft() (s = 0x400 + idx, slice d[s:s+256], IV = d[s-16:s]) and decrypt the probes with a synthetic AES-256-CBC container with a known key, then compare to the requested plaintext
notes: Only idx % 16 == 0 works; at idx=0,16 the requested plaintext came back, at idx=30, 1490063 and 1490319 it did not (a spliced ciphertext mid-block makes D() pseudorandom). The farm's own worklist range(0,ZIP_LEN,256) is aligned by luck, but every ad-hoc tail read was not: the saved map has 308 of 327 bytes (94%) at misaligned offsets, including the whole 30..82 run and the 256-byte 1490063..1490319 run. Consequence: FIRMWARE_ANALYSIS.md 65.7 (the 'ground truth' cross-check) was circular and 65.10 (no central directory in the last 512 bytes) is void. Corrected readable window is 16*floor(idx/16).

hypothesis: The device's log-message buffer caps a leaked oracle window at 65 bytes
test: Parse all surviving captures as C0/routing/type/len_be32/escaped-payload frames (toolkit/opzframe.py) and take the payload-length distribution
notes: opzraw3.bin: 1253 frames, max payload 128, walk consumes 78894/78915 bytes (100.0%); opzautocycle.raw: 12 frames, max 128; genuine console_upgrade_1_2_45.bin: 170 frames, max 103 (never reaches the ceiling). The single leak frame lands exactly on 128 with the arithmetic closing exactly: 4 (tick) + 58 ('[26-10-10 17:39:08] bootdisk: failed to find .zip file in ') + 65 (name) + 1 (NUL) = 128. Two independent leaks both measured exactly 65 bytes ending 2e 2e. So the IV-mask trick cannot raise throughput: the ceiling is ~65 bytes per window regardless of masking, full decode is 1490575/65 = 22932 windows (not 5800-9000) and every estimate built on 256 bytes per window is wrong.

hypothesis: parse_cycle() correctly delimits and decodes a leaked window
test: Read the frame stop condition and escape handling in opzfarm.py, then measure routing-byte frequency in the genuine capture
notes: It copies raw bytes without undoing the 7D escape and stops only at 'C0 2E 04'; but routing 0x1E is the common log routing (151 of 170 frames in console_upgrade_1_2_45.bin) and 0x2E the rare one (19), so the guard covers the uncommon case and a following frame header can be absorbed into a window and shift every later offset. Correct decoding (reconstruct frames, undo 7D->byte^0x20, isolate text, then unmask) is implemented in ~/.opz-decode/toolkit/opzframe.py.

hypothesis: Byte coverage or zip_walk() validates the assembled payload map
test: Read opzassemble.py: it zero-fills unknown offsets and zip_walk() rejects any local header with a nonempty name
notes: zip_walk() hard-codes the nameless-archive assumption as a validation rule ('local header has a N-byte name (archive is nameless)'), so it cannot validate an ordinary zip; unknown offsets are filled with zeros and then the header fields are printed from that invented buffer, which is how the 'empty entry name' claim was produced. A validator must not assume the format it is meant to test. Separately opzfarm.py:advance() moves an interval start forward by one when a probe produced nothing, silently deleting unknown bytes; the saved state is already missing 19,20,21,82,83,84 and 1490323-1490325.

hypothesis: Engine .engine files are a flat Blackfin image based at 0x11a00000
test: Walk all 21 engines as 16-byte blackfin boot headers (code,dest,count,arg) and check chain continuity and EOF
notes: All 21 walk as loader-block chains and every stream ends exactly at EOF; e.g. analoga.engine block 0 code=0xadcd5000 dest=0x11a00000 count=0 arg=0x1998 then dest=0x81b93800 count=56 then dest=0x81b93838 count=5136 (dest[i+1] == dest[i]+count[i]). 0x11a00000 is the L1 SRAM base used as a zero-length block destination, not a magic, and the first block's arg equals filesize-16 for all 21 (mistaken for a payload size). Consequence: RETX - image_base is not a file offset, and none of the recorded crash addresses 0x80117BAA / 0x8002C438 / 0x11A03838 / 0x11A02586 lies in any engine's load range, so the crash is in OS/L1 code rather than a plugin.

hypothesis: The recorded 0x11a00000/plugin framework model explains the crash addresses
test: Compare the four recorded crash addresses against the 21 engines' actual load destination ranges
notes: No engine load range contains any of the four addresses, so the plugin-framework reading does not place the fault; treat the crash as OS/L1 code and translate through the OS member's own block destination map once it is recovered.

hypothesis: The confirmed wordlist/KDF key negatives are invalidated by the disputed zip seed
test: Check whether ~/.opz-decode/opzstage1.c verifies the known plaintext filename block as well as the seed
notes: The key miner checks E_k(known plaintext) == C0x300 against the independently known front slice, so a wrong or spliced payload seed does not affect that negative; there is still no positive evidence for a human passphrase. Do not restart dictionary/KDF work on the strength of the seed dispute alone.

hypothesis: The known '50 4b 03 04 14 00 c0 1e 04 ...' seed is genuine payload plaintext
test: Read aligned payload window 0 with the corrected frame decoder and compare byte-for-byte
notes: The aligned read returned 50 4b 03 04 14 00 00 00 08 00 62 70 7f 54 47 9c 68 3c c9 00: 12 of the old seed's 19 bytes differ and the old bytes 6-18 were a console frame header (c0 1e 04 .. 49). DECISIVE INTERNAL PROOF that it was never a leak: the old constant contains NULs at offsets 9,10,11,18 and both the device's printf('%s') and parse_cycle() stop at a NUL, so no parser could have produced it - it was hand-pasted into GROUND_TRUTH and then re-asserted by every check run. Raw evidence: ~/.opz-decode/raws/w0_masked_20261010-193009.bin.

hypothesis: The archive is an ordinary zip whose first entry is Deflate with a real build date
test: Decode the first local file header from the aligned window-0 read
notes: PK\x03\x04, version needed 20, flags 0x0000 (no data descriptor, so local sizes are real and the chain is walkable), method 8 (DEFLATE), DOS time 0x7062 / date 0x547f = 2022-03-31 14:03:04, crc32 0x3c689c47, csize starts 0xc9 with a genuine NUL at offset 19. Every field self-consistent. This supersedes the whole 'flags 0x1ec0 / method 4 / nameless archive / no central directory' chain, which was derived from the bad seed (66.12).

hypothesis: The archive's first entry has an empty name and the components are order-identified
test: Re-derive the name from a correctly decoded local header (namelen at offsets 26-27, name at offset 30)
notes: The claim came from the hand-pasted seed plus a control read at idx 30 (==14 mod 16, misaligned) plus zip_walk's hard-coded nameless assumption (66.4). Window 0's header is an ordinary header with flags 0; namelen is not yet read, so the expectation is now a NAMED archive, and window 16 completes the header and should expose the first entry's name.

hypothesis: The oracle's IV mask can only be XOR 0x01
test: Read the stop byte of a window whose first block contains a true 0x01, then choose a different IV delta
notes: Read #2 stalled at window offset 7 with the byte printed 0x00 inside the masked block, i.e. the true byte was 0x01: under ^0x01 a true 0x01 becomes 0x00 and stops the print. The IV is ours, so block 0 can be shifted by ANY delta; a block is unreadable only if it contains a byte equal to the delta, and with 16 bytes and 240 usable deltas one can always be chosen. Encoded as MASK_DELTA in opzfarm.py and opzw0.py --delta N (66.13).

hypothesis: The archive's components are named files under a firmware/ directory
test: Decode a complete local file header from an aligned oracle window
notes: Read #3 (window 16, delta 2) gave the complete first header: crc32 0x3c689c47, csize 201, usize 315, namelen 21, extralen 0, name at offset 30 = 'firmware/versions.txt', entry data starting exactly at 51 = 30+21+0 with high-entropy deflate output. Replaces the earlier 'empty name / order-identified components' claim, which came from the hand-pasted seed and a misaligned control read. Raw evidence: ~/.opz-decode/raws/w16_d2_20261010-194013.bin.

hypothesis: A capped console leak yields 65 bytes of payload
test: Check the tail of every capped leak against every short leak in the durable captures
notes: Every capped leak (3/3) ends with 2e 2e and no short leak does, and the byte arithmetic closes exactly: 4 tick + 58 text + 63 data + 2 marker + 1 NUL = 128. So the logger truncates at 128 and appends a '..' marker: a capped read yields 63 real bytes, and the 2 bytes it overwrites must be re-read from an overlapping window. parse_cycle() now strips the marker (LAST['marker']), opzsim reproduces it, and opzcheck.sh asserts the invariant on all durable captures. Without this the map would have absorbed two bogus 0x2e bytes per capped window.

hypothesis: The first entry of the archive is the OS image
test: Read csize/usize from the first local header
notes: csize 201 / usize 315 for firmware/versions.txt - a tiny text-ish component, not the OS. The OS member still has to be found, which is what the central directory at the tail is for (or walking the local headers, one read per entry, jumping by csize).

hypothesis: The archive's zip offsets are biased by the 0x400 .zfw header
test: Check cd_offset + cd_size against the EOCD position
notes: cd_offset 1487649 + cd_size 2904 = 1490553, exactly the EOCD's own payload position, so the zip's offsets are payload-relative and carry no bias. An earlier hand transcription of the same 15 bytes suggested a +0x400 bias; that was an arithmetic slip of one byte and is retracted here.

hypothesis: The archive contains 31 named components whose full index is recoverable by the oracle
test: Decode the zip end-of-central-directory tail from an aligned oracle window
notes: Read #4 (window 1490560, delta 1) gave 00 1f 00 1f 00 58 0b 00 00 21 b3 16 00 00 00 = cd_disk 0, entries on disk 31, total 31, cd_size 2904, cd_offset 1487649, comment 0. The layout verifies three ways: cd_offset+cd_size = 1490553 = the EOCD position = 1490575-22 = payload end. The central directory occupies payload 1487649..1490552 at ~93.7 bytes per record. Raw evidence: ~/.opz-decode/raws/w1490560_d1_20261010-194446.bin.

hypothesis: The whole OS image can be recovered through the console oracle
test: Divide the OS member's likely size by the measured 63 bytes per power cycle
notes: MEASURED 2026-10-10: the oracle leaks the decrypted ARCHIVE, and every entry has method 8 (Deflate), so a member's payload offset holds its COMPRESSED stream (read #8 returned high-entropy deflate bytes at opz.ldr's start). A deflate stream cannot be read partially, so content costs the whole csize: opz.ldr's 466,903 bytes = 7,412 power cycles at 63 B/read. The oracle cannot deliver the image, and neither can the crash logs (no instruction/memory/stack dump: 0 hex-dump lines). Hardware or TE service is required for the OS image. What it CAN deliver is the 2904-byte central directory (~46 cycles), small members, and targeted ~64-byte reads. Plan accordingly: locate the OS member, read its Blackfin block map (~300 bytes), compute the offset of RETX 0x80117BAA and read only that window.

hypothesis: The OS image is firmware/blackfin/bin/opz.ldr, a Blackfin loader stream
test: Complete entry 3's local header with one aligned oracle window and read its name
notes: Read #7 (window 336, delta 1) returned the complete entry-3 header in one window as the 66.16 recipe predicted: csize 466903, usize 828136, namelen 29, extralen 0, name 'firmware/blackfin/bin/opz.ldr', data at payload 377, next header at 467280. The .ldr extension plus the engine container format (66.6) means the fault address maps to a file offset through the loader block headers, so RETX 0x80117BAA can be disassembled from a handful of targeted reads instead of decoding 809 KB. Raw evidence: ~/.opz-decode/raws/w336_d1_20261010-195245.bin.

hypothesis: The archive's entries are ordered metadata-first then OS
test: Read entries 1-3 in order from the local headers
notes: Entry 1 firmware/versions.txt (315 B), entry 2 firmware/firmware.version (9 B), entry 3 firmware/blackfin/bin/opz.ldr (809 KB). Entries 1 and 2 share the DOS stamp 2022-03-31 14:03:04, so the archive was written in one pass. This makes a name-driven walk cheap: the components follow the two metadata files.

hypothesis: The .ldr loader block map can be read to map RETX 0x80117BAA to a file offset
test: Read the first loader header from opz.ldr's payload start
notes: The plan assumed the .ldr content is visible in the archive plaintext. It is not: the entry is Deflate-compressed (method 8), so the payload holds the compressed stream (read #8, window 384, returned high-entropy deflate bytes). Reading the block map would require all 466,903 compressed bytes (7,412 power cycles). RETRACTED.

hypothesis: The OP-Z crash log contains an instruction or memory dump around the fault
test: Scan crashlogs/latest/system.log and crash01.log for hex dumps and dump keywords
notes: 0 lines with more than 8 hex bytes (the two matches are garbled UTF-8 lines), and 0 occurrences of disasm, opcode, dump, 'code:' or 'stack:'. The crash record gives iid, fault address, RETX, callstack frames and registers, but no code bytes, so it cannot substitute for the OS image.

hypothesis: Content mode plus the MIDI file-transport service can read internal device files (such as the decompressed OS component)
test: Run the OP-Z in content mode (power on holding TRACK) and use the $35 file-request messages with fileId = crc32(utf8(lowercase(path)))
notes: The file transport is an OS-level service, which is why it was previously ruled out (normal mode crashes before MidiInit). Content mode runs the same OS successfully, so the service should be alive there, and the device is documented to both serve ($35 -> $53 packets) and receive files, with arbitrary paths addressed by crc32 of the lowercased path. If it serves the internal /yaffs2 tree, this is a host-side read path to the decompressed components - including the OS image - that the console oracle cannot provide. Raw material: op-z-sysex docs (clean-room-file-transport.md), FIRMWARE_ANALYSIS file-transport section.

hypothesis: The console oracle recovers correct member content for small zip entries
test: Read entry 2's 11-byte Deflate stream through the oracle and inflate it
notes: Read #9 (window 304, delta 1) returned entry 2's 11 compressed bytes (33 d4 33 d2 33 31 d5 36 e0 02 00); raw-Deflate inflating them yields exactly b'1.2.45+0\n' = 9 bytes, matching the header's usize field byte-for-byte. The device's bytes also place entry 3's PK signature at 318, the offset computed from csize, and read #5 and read #9 agree on the overlapping bytes 307-316. This proves the whole chain (frame decode, unmask, delta, offsets, sparse map) on hardware - the first real component content recovered from the device. Raw evidence: ~/.opz-decode/raws/w304_d1_20261010-200044.bin.

hypothesis: firmware/firmware.version contains the OS version string
test: Inflate the entry's stream
notes: Content is '1.2.45+0' plus a newline (9 bytes). The '+0' suffix is a build/variant marker not previously known from the .zfw header, which reports only the plaintext length.

hypothesis: Update mode exposes a USB-MIDI port
test: List CoreMIDI input/output names while the unit is in update mode
notes: mido.get_input_names() and get_output_names() are both EMPTY in update mode, so the file service is not reachable there at all; it is an OS-level service. Combined with the crash in normal mode, content mode is the only candidate mode, and whether it exposes MIDI is the open question.

hypothesis: The clean-room file transport works on this unit's firmware version
test: Compare the reference project's device-proof firmware version against this unit's
notes: ~/.opz-decode/refs/op-z-sysex documents its file transport as device-proven on 2026-07-26 with OP-Z firmware 1.2.45+, and this unit runs firmware.version = '1.2.45+0', so the transport implementation matches the running version. A read-only fetch tool is built at ~/.opz-decode/toolkit/opzfetch.py (sends only $51 and $35, never $52/$53 uploads).

hypothesis: Setting disable_start_sound=true lets the boot proceed past the crash
test: Edit config/general.json on the mounted content disk, boot content mode to import it, then boot normally and diff the fresh crash log
notes: VOID AS RUN (2026-10-10): the content-disk channel does not apply edits. The follow-up control read shows the disk's general.json is byte-identical to the ORIGINAL baseline (336 B, sha 4eb733170616, disable_start_sound=false), the 335-byte edited file is gone, import.log stayed empty (no [IMPORT STARTED] cycle), and general.json carries the device's unset-clock mtime - i.e. the device WRITES its config out at boot and clobbers the disk copy. So the internal value was never changed and the crash result says nothing about this setting. The corrected test needs the plain-zip traversal write of ../user/config/general.json. The config-TREE evidence from the same run (that /yaffs2/user/config/ exists) is unaffected and still disproves the missing-config theory.

hypothesis: A missing /yaffs2/user/config/ explains the crash
test: Compare the baseline and fresh system.log opendir failures
notes: The baseline boot logged 'filemanager: opendir failed: /yaffs2/user/config/' while the fresh boot does not, i.e. the config directory (with a complete all-defaults general.json) now EXISTS, and the crash is byte-identical in its fault fields. The missing-config theory is closed on the device side, independently of which values the config holds.

hypothesis: A pre-1.1.12 firmware build boots normally on this unit
test: Install an older .zfw from before the 1.1.12 lineage (1.1.5/1.1.9 era) via the normal staged upgrade and observe
notes: Every OS build tested so far (1.2.45, 1.1.12) crashes with the same iid, one at RETX 0x80117baa and the other at 0x8010ea52, so both come from the same lineage. A pre-1.1.12 archive is the only untried version and the only cheap recovery shot that needs no special access: if any older build initialises successfully, the unit is usable again. Requires locating such an archive online.

hypothesis: Editing config on the content disk changes the device's internal config
test: Edit config/general.json on the mounted content disk, boot content mode, then read the disk's copy back
notes: The device reconstructs/clobbers these files at boot: after the content-mode boot the disk's general.json was byte-identical to the original baseline (my 335-byte edit gone) and carried the DEVICE's unset-clock mtime (Dec 30 2017), while untouched midi.json kept its 2024 mtime. import.log recorded no [IMPORT STARTED] cycle. The content disk is an OUTBOUND mirror of the internal config (so it is a good way to READ the internal state) but a write to it is discarded. Internal config changes must use the plain-zip traversal write, which is how the earlier config variants in the notes were actually applied.

hypothesis: The content disk mirrors the internal /yaffs2/user/ config, so it can be read to inspect device state
test: Compare the disk's config files and mtimes against the device's own save path
notes: The disk's config/general.json holds the device's own saved value with a device-clock mtime, and the disk's config/ directory corresponds to the internal /yaffs2/user/config/ that the boot log now opens successfully. This is a free, host-side read of part of the internal user tree whenever the unit is in content mode.

hypothesis: A pre-1.1.12 OP-Z firmware can still be obtained
test: Probe TE's _software/op-z/z_firmware_*.zfw URL pattern across plausible version numbers
notes: Seventeen builds return HTTP 200, including 1.1.9 (822,960 B) which is older than any archive previously available locally; 1.0.x and 1.1.0-1.1.8 all 404 so 1.1.9 is the floor. 1.1.9 and 1.1.17 are downloaded to opz-firmware-notes/old-firmware/ and verified as well-formed containers: keyidx 0xFF and 0x400 + ceil(plaintext_len/16)*16 equal to the file size exactly. The URL pattern was recovered from the Wayback index; the official app exposes only account and DLC APIs, no firmware URL.

hypothesis: The oldest available firmware boots normally on this bricked unit

Installer tool ~/.opz-decode/toolkit/opzinstall.py (cleans other archives first, since the bootloader installs the first firmware-named candidate in FAT order). Risk: installs 1.1.9's bootloader too; mitigations already proven on this unit are the A/B bootloader slots and repeated successful 1.2.45 reflashes. hypothesis: A genuine older TE archive installs through the device's own updater
test: Stage z_firmware_1_1_9.zfw via toolkit/opzinstall.py and read the updater's console log
notes: The 1.1.9 install completed every stage: decrypt 772096/822960, extract 1566161/1566161, copied 6 files, content OK (0), os OK (0), bootloader OK (0) written to A/B index 1, ble Already installed (-200), psoc rows 0-511. The device's updater independently confirmed keyidx 0xff and 0x400 + ceil(821931/16)*16 = 822960, and version.txt now reports os/bootloader/keyboard 1.1.9. The updater's component list is content (6 files), os, bootloader, ble, psoc, and the decrypted name field is firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip, the same string 1.1.27's archive carries.

hypothesis: The OP-Z archive's encrypted name field differs between firmware versions
test: Compare the updater's 'filename found' line across staged archives (1.1.9 vs 1.1.27)
notes: 1.1.9's updater reports firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip, byte-identical to the name 1.1.27's archive reports, so the encrypted name carries one constant string across the 1.1.x line rather than a per-version identifier; it is the bootloader's filename check that requires it, not a version marker.

hypothesis: 1.1.9 crashes like 1.1.12 and 1.2.45, at the same function
test: Install 1.1.9 from TE, boot normally, and compare iid, RETX and callstack against the 1.2.45 and 1.1.12 baselines

hypothesis: A pre-1.1.12 firmware boots on this unit
test: Install 1.1.9 and power on normally
notes: 1.1.9 (the oldest build TE still serves) installs cleanly and crashes with iid 0x00130026, RETX 0x8010ea4c and the same DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000. The firmware-downgrade recovery shot is exhausted; the crash follows the code, not the version.

hypothesis: Normal-mode boots fail while content-mode boots succeed because the fault is in the normal-mode-only init sequence
test: Reconstruct every boot in the device's rolling system.log and classify by contentmanager/snakesystem presence and outcome
notes: Ten reconstructed boots completed and idled ~100 s before a PSOC-requested power-off; all ten are content-mode (they run contentmanager and mass_storage and never print 'snakesystem:'). test: Stage a plain zip named firmware_bin_only_with_bootloader.zip carrying ../user/config/general.json and ../user/samplepacks/user/<id>.engine and let the updater extract it, then boot normally and diff the crash log

hypothesis: The §24 engine write lets the unit boot the application

notes: The next normal boot reached the startup animation and the track-selection UI and responded to the TRACK button, and the app initialised completely: sequencer (79 ms), audio init, MIDI (config/midi.json loaded), codec start, audio start, jack detect, finalize, and the sequencer/filemanager tasks. It then ran ~9 s before faulting. The earlier fault was a null DATA read at 0x00000000 during init (iid 0x00130026); the new one is an INSTRUCTION CPLB miss with RETX: 0 (iid 0x0013002c), i.e. a call through a null function pointer from the running sequencer. This supersedes the notes' conclusion that no host-supplyable file changes the crash.

hypothesis: The unit can produce audio again
test: Play notes on the repaired unit and listen

hypothesis: The plug layer (plugs.json) is the cause of the PLAY crash

hypothesis: The remaining PLAY crash is in the power/battery path

notes: The log shows 'main: requesting psoc error log' immediately before the quiet 31 s that ends in the fault, and healthy boots on this session repeatedly end with 'Going to charging state' / 'PSOC requested POWER_MODE_REQUEST_POWER_OFF' after ~100 s, which is what a flat or failing battery looks like. hypothesis: The remaining PLAY crash is the power/battery path
test: Charge the unit fully, then boot and press PLAY - compare with a flat-battery boot
notes: The user reports the unit is fully charged, so a flat battery is not the trigger. The PSOC/power lines in the log ('main: requesting psoc error log') remain unexplained but the charge state is not the cause. The leading replacement is the slot map: the previous payload pointed all 16 tracks at plug 10 (a SYNTH), including tracks 8-11 which are the FX slots the fxmanager asks for (34/36/37/39); an FX chain holding a non-FX plugin is a plausible PLAY crash, and it also explains the newly odd track-switching. hypothesis: dlm rejects an engine binary loaded into more than one module slot

The real variable is the memoryslot, which sets the window dlm accepts: those five had no known slot so the builder passed 0, giving them the smallest window that their code destinations (0x81b32000-0x81c07c00) cannot fit.

hypothesis: The official engine binaries and their memory slots are publicly obtainable

hypothesis: Defining the device's own default-map plug ids with official memory slots makes every track sound and removes the track-select crashes

hypothesis: The last crashing track is a plugin with a null callback rather than a missing file
