notes: The fault is iid 0x0013002c / ADI_EXC_INSTR_CPLB_MISS / ICPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000 / RETX 0x00000000 about 30 s after boot with nothing logged in between, so no host file or log line names the track. Mechanism hypothesis: the nine ids with no published plug record (15/21/28/36/37/60/70/80/100) get default flags/trackmask and no presets, while the seven with real catalogue records (13/14/17/25/31/34/39) are complete. Five engines remain unused and placeable for a substitution test: dist 78, electric 77, ministringshort 82, sampleplayergain 10, tapetwo 9.

hypothesis: The silent, crashing track 1 is plug 13 trying to sampler without a sample pack
test: Set samples='redmountKicks.aif' with trackmask=1 on plug 13, install the pack at /yaffs2/user/samplepacks/user/, then boot and press track 1 and PLAY
notes: Track 1 is the kick. samplepacks/1-kick/01/~13.engine names plug 13 for that slot and the device's default map sends track 1 to plug 13. The payload gave plug 13 engine sampleplayergain (correct, it is the drum engine) but samples='' and the default trackmask 240, i.e. a synth-group mask on a drum track. sampleplayergain plugs in every catalogue carry a samples value (TeKicks.aif, CuckooSnares.aif, redmountKicks.aif) resolved under samplepacks/user/ (0x757f9, format %s%saif 0x78560), which explains one 'sampleloader: No samples found for id 0' per unprovisioned drum track and the NULL+0x2c0 load on PLAY. Staged: extract 1,006,678/1,006,678, 0 failures.

hypothesis: TE publishes OP-Z sample packs through the public DLC file API
test: Scan every DLC record's files[] for kind=opz-sample and download each api_path without auth
notes: The redmount DLC 288ecfdc-9a3c-41c9-b0ef-6ce9b2ea32a9 has four files of kind opz-sample, mime application/opz-sample; all four return HTTP 200 with no key: redmountKicks.aif 891,612 B, redmountSnares.aif 817,450 B, redmountPerc.aif 944,000 B, redmountFX.aif 1,028,170 B, each a genuine FORM....AIFF. They are the only opz-sample files in all 28 records; the teenage DLC (plugs 121-124) publishes a hero image only, so TeKicks.aif and its siblings are not obtainable this way.

hypothesis: Plug trackmask is a track bitmask and a plug on a track its mask excludes cannot play
test: Read trackmask values against the pack-slot marker ids and the app's invalid-plug string
notes: Bit N-1 = track N: 1/2/4/8 = drum tracks 1-4 individually (te-kicks/snares/perc/fx 121-124), 12 = tracks 3-4 (vinyl 71), 240 = the synth group 5-8, 256/2048 = tracks 9/12 (delay 34, chorus 39), 768 = tracks 9-10 (rymd 35, dist 99, crush 109), 0 = not a track plug (dmx basic 146, performance 147). The app carries 'Track %d has invalid plug, can't play note' at .rodata 0x7a70f. The repair payload had set trackmask 240 on all sixteen plugs, so every drum plug claimed the synth group.

hypothesis: The content disk's samplepack tree independently reproduces the device's default slot map
test: Read the ~<plugid>.engine marker in slot 01 of each samplepacks/<track>-<name> pack
notes: 1-kick->13, 2-snare->14, 3-perc->15, 4-fx->17, 5-bass->21, 6-lead->25, 7-arpeggio->28, 8-chord->31, i.e. exactly the ids 13,14,15,17,21,25,28,31 that the instrument manager asks for, in track order. Slots 02-04 of all four synth packs hold plugs 10, 14 and 17 (analoga, organ, ep), so a plug id is not tied to one track - it may occupy any pack slot whose trackmask admits that track.

hypothesis: The normal-mode OS file service is live and is what the iPhone app uses
test: Read system.log around the PLAY boot and identify the server id 37201 the device connects to
notes: The device logs 'fileclient: FileClient: send connection request to server 37201', then 'filesync: got new file request: 0 (part 0)' and '1', then 'send file part /yaffs2/user/settings/slotConfiguration.json 0' and 'plugs.json' parts 0/50/100. 37201 is not our tool (0x4242 = 16962); the BLE central 'Connected to central 46:23:22:b6:c3:7b' is logged 20 s earlier, so 37201 is the phone app. This retires the earlier 'the file service never answers' conclusion: the service answers, our host was on the wrong transport at the wrong moment.

hypothesis: A plug's samples field names a pack the device really tries to load
test: Give plug 13 samples='redmountKicks.aif', boot, and read the boot log
notes: The boot went from one 'sampleloader: No samples found for id 0' per drum track to 628 alternating 'libaiff: AIFF_ReadOpen failed: failed to open' + 'yaffsfs: yaffs: error: ENOENT' lines in a ~35 s retry loop (crash01, 20:25:20-20:25:55) ending at callstack 0x8002c438. So the field drives a real file open; it simply is not finding the pack. Side effect: the flood pushed the fault registers out of the 7152-byte dump, and the flood is itself a plausible crash contributor.

hypothesis: The internal sample-pack path is samplepacks/user/<name>
test: Place redmountKicks.aif at /yaffs2/user/samplepacks/user/ and read the resulting boot log
notes: Still 628 ENOENT/AIFF_ReadOpen pairs with the file present, so the playback loader does not read that location. The disassembly explains why: 'samplepacks/user/' (0x757f9, 17 chars) is the second of two candidates tried by the import function around 0x101060, alongside 'samplepacks/' + name (0x78fec, 11 chars); that function also carries the 0x1800001 (24 MB+1) sample budget and the strings '  importing %s...' and '  Can't import %s, sample memory full', so samplepacks/user/ is the content-disk spelling and the internal playback location remains unproven.

hypothesis: Seeding every candidate sample path in one write finds the loader's real location
test: Write redmountKicks.aif (891,612 B) to samplepacks/, samplepacks/user/, samplepacks/1-kick/ and samplepacks/1-kick/01/ under /yaffs2/user/, then boot
notes: Reaches extract 3,681,514/3,681,514 with 0 'Failed to extract'. Costs ~4 s of extraction instead of one power cycle per guess. If the flood disappears and track 1 sounds, the placement question is answered; if the flood persists, the path is outside /yaffs2/user/ and the content disk is the only write channel that can reach it.

hypothesis: The four sample copies never physically landed in /yaffs2/user/
test: Boot content mode and read the exported samplepacks tree, which mirrors the internal /yaffs2/user/, to see whether redmountKicks.aif is present
notes: The loader chain is now fully named: PlugManager::getSamplePackPath(id) (a std::map lookup) -> FileManager::getAbsolutePath (abs = FileManager+0x270 + rel) -> AIFF_OpenFile(abs,1) -> SampleLoader::readSamples with isUser = strstr(abs,'samplepacks/user/'). The only in-binary composer of 'samplepacks/' (0x78fec) is the import function, referenced once, so the map entry probably carries the plug's samples value as-is and the attempted path is <root>/redmountKicks.aif. Two explanations remain and the logs cannot separate them: the writes did not land, or the FileManager root is not /yaffs2/user/.

hypothesis: The 891 kB sample pack never physically landed in /yaffs2/user/
test: Read the content-mode boot log for the sample-memory accounting line
notes: The log reads 'contentmanager: Calculating used sample memory: 958 kB' where it used to read 88 kB; the 870 kB delta is the 891,612-byte redmountKicks.aif plus rounding. So the file is present and the content manager walks and counts it. The earlier system.log flood is therefore a path-resolution difference between the playback loader (PlugManager::getSamplePackPath + FileManager::getAbsolutePath) and the import, not a missing file.

hypothesis: Writing a file inside a factory pack directory breaks content mode
test: Place redmountKicks.aif at samplepacks/1-kick/ and samplepacks/1-kick/01/, then boot content mode
notes: Content mode crashes before mounting: iid 0x00130026, ADI_EXC_DATA_CPLB_MISS, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000001, RETX 0x80033fd6, right after 'mass_storage: create and mount FAT' and the benign 'opendir failed: /yaffs2/user/rejected/'. Callstack 0x8002c438, 0x11a03838, 0x11a02586, 0x8003691c, 0x80037722, 0x8002d2e8, 0x80134a04 - the first three are the shared dispatcher frames, the rest are new mass-storage frames. A factory pack directory holds slot dirs plus one_sample_pack_per_slot.plz; the FAT-export walker dereferences null on the unexpected entry. Fix: blank both copies to 0 bytes (the updater cannot delete, but truncation reclaims the space) and keep the pack only at samplepacks/<name> and samplepacks/user/<name>, the two locations the import function actually tries.

hypothesis: A file planted inside the factory pack tree is what crashes content mode
test: Truncate the copies at samplepacks/1-kick/ and samplepacks/1-kick/01/ to 0 bytes, then boot content mode
notes: The crash is byte-identical: iid 0x00130026, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000001, RETX 0x80033fd6, callstack 0x8002c438, 0x11a03838, 0x11a02586, 0x8003691c, 0x80037722, 0x8002d2e8, 0x80134a04, still right after 'mass_storage: create and mount FAT'. The contentmanager line still reads 958 kB, i.e. the tree walk and the pack read both succeed, and every faulting frame is OS mass-storage code with no app frame present. So the pack's placement inside the pack tree is not the trigger.

hypothesis: The FileManager root is /yaffs2/, so a plug's samples value resolves to /yaffs2/<name>
test: Write redmountKicks.aif to /yaffs2/redmountKicks.aif via the entry '../redmountKicks.aif' (one '..' from /yaffs2/upgrade/), truncate every copy under /yaffs2/user/, and boot both normal and content mode
notes: FileManager::getAbsolutePath is root + rel, and a pack under /yaffs2/user/samplepacks/** is never opened by the playback loader, so the root is probably /yaffs2/ rather than /yaffs2/user/. That reading explains every absolute path in the app's logs: 'Failed to load project /yaffs2/user/projects/project09.opz' = root + 'user/projects/project09.opz'. It predicts the pack is opened at /yaffs2/redmountKicks.aif, which is also outside the content tree and therefore cannot disturb the FAT export that content mode builds. Two '..' segments would reach past the yaffsfs root and fail, so '../<name>' is the only way out of the user tree.

hypothesis: The FileManager root is /yaffs2/
test: Write the pack to /yaffs2/redmountKicks.aif via one '..' and read the sample-memory line
notes: The content-mode boot still reports 'Calculating used sample memory: 88 kB', not 958 kB, so the pack at the yaffs root is not read either. Combined with the pack never being found under /yaffs2/user/samplepacks/**, the root is still unidentified; the pack must live somewhere inside /yaffs2/user/.

hypothesis: A plug samples field naming an unloadable pack is what crashes content mode
test: Revert plug 13 to samples='' / trackmask=240 (its exact pre-regression state), blank the stray /yaffs2 file, then boot content mode
notes: This is the one change present in every crashing content-mode boot and absent from the state that preceded the regression. The boot log shows the causal chain: 'yaffsfs: yaffs: error: ENOENT' (the pack open fails), 'contentmanager: Calculating used sample memory: 88 kB', 'mass_storage: create and mount FAT', then the fault at DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000001 / RETX 0x80033fd6. A null sample-pack object left by the failed load is dereferenced while the FAT export walks the pack tree. If content mode recovers, the samples field is the trigger; if not, the leftover 0-byte entries and the samplepacks/user/ directory are, and those can only be removed by the file transport's sync manifest.

hypothesis: A plug samples field naming an unloadable pack makes content mode unreachable
test: Revert plug 13 to samples='' / trackmask=240 and boot content mode
notes: Content mode mounts again. The crashing boots all carried samples='redmountKicks.aif' with no loadable pack, and their log chain is explicit: 'yaffsfs: yaffs: error: ENOENT' (open fails), 'contentmanager: Calculating used sample memory: 88 kB', 'mass_storage: create and mount FAT', then the fault at DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000001 / RETX 0x80033fd6. A failed load leaves a null sample-pack object and the FAT export walks the same pack tree; every faulting frame is OS mass-storage code with no app frame. Rule: set a plug's samples field only once the pack is actually present.

hypothesis: The sample files or their placement were what crashed content mode
test: Remove the pack from /yaffs2/user/ entirely (memory drops to the 88 kB baseline) and boot content mode
notes: With the pack gone from the user tree and the accounting back at 88 kB, the crash was byte-identical in every field (iid 0x00130026, FA 0x00000001, RETX 0x80033fd6, same seven frames). Neither the placements, the duplicate copies, nor their 0-byte truncations had any effect on content mode. Supersedes the narrower conclusions of 66.35 and 66.36, both of which attacked the wrong variable.

hypothesis: The content disk is a full mirror of /yaffs2/user/
test: Compare the mounted export against what the updater wrote
notes: It is a curated export: config/, projects/, samplepacks/, bounces/, rejected/ plus how_to_dmx.txt, how_to_import.txt and import.log. settings/ and engines/ are NOT exported, and samplepacks/ shows only the eight <track>-<name> pack dirs, so the updater's .aif files and samplepacks/user/ directory do not appear. The disk therefore confirms config/projects/samplepacks state and proves nothing about plugs.json, slotConfiguration.json or the engine binaries.

hypothesis: Disk space was a limiting factor for the content export
test: Read the mounted volume's capacity
notes: The content volume is 33 MiB with 1.9 MiB used and 31 MiB free. The 3.6 MB of duplicate packs written earlier was about 11% of the volume, so no space-based explanation for any failure survives - including the theories about the FAT image being oversized.

hypothesis: The §24 updater write demonstrably lands and is re-exported by the device
test: Write config/dmx.json through the updater, then boot content mode and inspect config/
notes: The mounted volume's config/ holds dmx.json at 782 B with a host timestamp, alongside the device's own general.json (335 B, Dec 30 2017) and midi.json (1 429 B). So the write landed in /yaffs2/user/config/ and the device re-exported it - the same channel that carries plugs.json, slotConfiguration.json and the engine binaries is confirmed against an independent read-back.

hypothesis: The content disk registers sample packs, whereas the updater's raw writes leave them inert
test: Read the eject sync log and compare against the loader behaviour for updater-written packs
notes: The eject prints 'contentmanager: Remove unused sample pack samplepacks/user/<file>' for every entry in samplepacks/user/ that no plug references, and it listed the staged redmountKicks.aif plus every ~<plugid>.engine ghost, then reported 'Calculating used sample memory: 0 kB'. So samplepacks/user/ is a garbage-collected user-pack area, the import runs on eject, and only the import produces a registered pack - which is why every updater-written pack was unreadable by the loader.

hypothesis: PLAY and the silent drum tracks are the same missing-sample fault
test: Read the log sequence immediately preceding the PLAY crash
notes: 'sampleloader: No samples found for id 0' appears at 20:46:03, 20:46:04 and 20:46:05, then at 20:46:09 the fault arrives with DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0 and RETX 0x80117baa. A 0x2c0 offset is a field on the sample object the lookup should have returned, so PLAY starts playback, the drum lookups return nothing and the voice allocation dereferences null. This also explains why the failing boot is the one with 'used sample memory: 0 kB'.

hypothesis: A pack placed in a factory slot directory needs no plugs.json change to reach its track
test: Put the kick pack in samplepacks/1-kick/01/ - the slot whose ~13.engine marker names plug 13 - and eject, then test track 1
notes: The disk's own layout carries the track-to-plug binding in the ~<plugid>.engine marker, so slot 01 of 1-kick belongs to plug 13. Placing the pack there should register it against that slot without any edit to settings/plugs.json, which also avoids the sample-reference-must-resolve rule that took content mode offline. The disk does not export settings/ or engines/, so those still require the updater.

hypothesis: Drum sample packs placed in factory slot directories are imported
test: Stage the four redmount packs at samplepacks/1-kick/01, 2-snare/01, 3-perc/01 and 4-fx/01, eject, and read the next boot
notes: The eject printed no removal for them, so they survive, but the next boot reads 'contentmanager: Calculating used sample memory: 0 kB' - nothing was registered. Slot directories hold the ~<plugid>.engine plug-binding markers only; audio placed there is inert. Meanwhile samplepacks/user/ is explicitly managed: in the earlier attempt the device printed 'Remove unused sample pack samplepacks/user/redmountKicks.aif', recognising the file as a pack and deleting it only because no plug referenced it.

hypothesis: A pack registers only when the pack file and a referencing plug arrive together
test: Write the packs to samplepacks/user/ and a settings/plugs.json referencing them onto the same content disk, then eject
notes: Two separate findings combine into this: the eject sync keeps only packs some plug's samples field names (66.41), and a samples reference that cannot resolve crashes the FAT export content mode builds (66.38). The reference must therefore be present at the eject, and the updater cannot supply it alone. Also established: a raw .aif written by the updater is never loadable because the import converts it - which is why every updater-placed pack produced 600+ AIFF_ReadOpen retries. The disk is the only channel that can deliver both at once.

hypothesis: The content disk can install sample packs
test: Stage the four redmount packs on the disk, eject, and read import.log plus the sample-space counter
notes: import.log lists the complete cycle: Reading content disk, Calculating used sample space (0.0/24.0 MB), Syncronizing rejected, config, projects, bounces, Rebuilding plug definitions. There is no sample step and the space counter never moved with four packs staged. Samples are not a disk content type; the runtime's own 'Remove unused sample pack' lines come from enumerating the internal samplepacks/user/, not from the import.

hypothesis: settings/plugs.json and settings/slotConfiguration.json can be delivered on the content disk
test: Write them to settings/ on the mounted disk, eject, and remount
notes: The remounted volume has no settings/ at all, and no .aif anywhere: the FAT is rebuilt from the curated export on every mount, so anything written outside the exported set is discarded. Both files were silently dropped while import.log still reported SUCCESS. Plug definitions and slot configuration can only travel through the updater.

hypothesis: The disk's samplepacks tree drives the device's plug-to-slot assignment
test: Compare the exported tree (samplepacks/<pack>/<slot>/~<plugid>.engine) against import.log's 'Rebuilding plug definitions...SUCCESS' step
notes: The import rebuilds plug definitions from the content disk, and the only plug-identity data on that disk is the ~<plugid>.engine marker in each slot directory (1-kick/01/~13.engine, 2-snare/01/~14.engine, 3-perc/01/~15.engine, 4-fx/01/~17.engine, 5-bass/01/~21.engine, 6-lead/01/~25.engine, 7-arpeggio/01/~28.engine, 8-chord/01/~31.engine). So the disk controls the plug-to-slot map even though it can carry neither plug records nor audio.

hypothesis: Factory drum pack names resolve from ROM without any file present
test: Give plug 13 a factory pack name such as TeKicks.aif and boot, watching for AIFF_ReadOpen retries and the sample-space counter
notes: On a healthy OP-Z the factory plugs carry samples values (TeKicks.aif, TeSnares.aif, CuckooKicks.aif ...) and no such file exists on the content disk, so those names must resolve from firmware. If a factory name resolves it avoids the whole deadlock; if it fails it will fail the same way ours did (repeated AIFF_ReadOpen failures), which is itself informative. Cheaper than building a BLE pusher and worth doing first.

hypothesis: The factory drum pack names (TeKicks.aif etc.) resolve from firmware
test: Give plugs 13/14/15/17 the catalogue's factory shape (sampleplayergain + TeKicks/TeSnares/TePercs/TeFX.aif + masks 1/2/4/8) and boot
notes: 593 'libaiff: AIFF_ReadOpen failed: failed to open' lines in the next boot, so a factory name is looked up as a file like any other and the factory drum packs are not resident in firmware at any path the loader knows. Reverted (FACTORY_DRUMS = False), which also restores track 3's analoga tone and keeps content mode safe.

hypothesis: The MIDI file transport is the only remaining channel that can register a sample pack
test: Audit every channel against live-device evidence
notes: Updater: plug definitions yes, audio no - writes never register a pack (600+ AIFF retries). Content disk: neither - settings/ is discarded on remount and import.log's fixed step list (rejected, config, projects, bounces, plug definitions) has no sample stage, with sample space stuck at 0.0/24.0 MB. Factory ROM names: 593 failed opens. Only the manufacturer transport remains, and it is proven on this unit today: the phone app served the device slotConfiguration.json and plugs.json at 20:19:39 over BLE (fileclient: send connection request to server 37201, filesync: send file part). Its mechanics are already documented here: $51 advertises a server, the device answers $34, $35 requests by fileId = crc32(lowercase(path)), $53 carries 200-byte parts, reserved ids 0/1/2, and a syncjob.json manifest drives the push.

hypothesis: The app's sync emptied the device's engine binaries, causing the track-select crash
test: Read the app sync log around the engine file requests and compare the finalize CRCs
notes: The log shows 'filesync: Ignore File request engines/organ.engine, same crc: 403f126c' followed by 'fileclient: invalid file crc, can't finalize /yaffs2/user/engines/organ.engine (0 != 403f126c)', and the same pair for ep, sampleplayergain, analoga, ministringshort, cluster, saw013a, fm003b, fdnreverb, crush, dist, chorus2 and tapetwo. A CRC of 0 means the file is empty, and the client state believing 'same crc' means the app never re-sends it. The missing engine leaves a null entry, so 'instrumentmanag: Can't load engine 17' is followed by iid 0x0013002c / ADI_EXC_INSTR_CPLB_MISS / ICPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0 / RETX 0 when that track is selected.

hypothesis: The official engine binaries match the CRCs the device expects, so they can be written back to satisfy the app
test: Compute crc32 of each engines-official/*.engine and compare with the expected values in the finalize error lines
notes: 13 of 13 match: analoga fe07077e, chorus2 9fa49506, cluster e9ebe2f2, crush 6a41b719, dist 879ce37a, ep 2dfa7db0, fdnreverb 9873b014, fm003b 6c9ffbd3, ministringshort 7412e200, organ 403f126c, sampleplayergain 26d66594, saw013a 671de54c, tapetwo 8a0f351c. So restoring the binaries lets the app's verification pass and unblocks the sync, which in turn lets the sample packs already sitting in /yaffs2/user/inbox/samplepacks/ apply.

hypothesis: The app, not the updater, must own settings/plugs.json and settings/slotConfiguration.json
test: Compare the app's sync behaviour against our updater-written JSON files
notes: The app drives its own definitions: it requests settings/slotConfiguration.json, imports plugs ('plugmanager: found plug to import, id:14 index:1') and rebuilds them. Our updater payloads were overwriting that state, so opzfix.py now has ENGINES_ONLY = True and writes only engines. Related new failure mode: a raw updater write can be emptied by the app's sync when the client state disagrees with the file contents, so the file is not merely ignored but truncated.

hypothesis: The track-1 crash comes from the plug table, not the engine binaries
test: Compare the crash signature against the plug map and re-stage plug 13 as sampleplayergain
notes: After the engines-only repair removed every 'instrumentmanag: Can't load engine' line, the same crash persisted: iid 0x0013002c, ADI_EXC_INSTR_CPLB_MISS, ICPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0, RETX 0. RETX 0 is a call through a null function pointer and iid 0x0013002c is the id already tied to the kick track, while the DLC catalogue's own plug 13 is chorus-80, an FX engine with no playable voice on a drum track. The app's plug import had landed on top of the earlier fix, so plug 13 was an FX engine again. Re-staged payload: plug 13 engines/sampleplayergain.engine with trackmask 1.

hypothesis: A drum plug carrying the catalogue's trackmask 240 can never play a note
test: Decode the trackmask bitmask for the four drum plugs and re-stage with 1/2/4/8
notes: trackmask is a bitmask whose bit N-1 selects track N: 1/2/4/8 are drum tracks 1-4 individually, 240 is the synth group (tracks 5-8), 256/1024/2048 are tracks 9/11/12. Every plug record taken from the DLC catalogue carries 240 for its synth-group purposes, so a drum plug given 240 mismatches its track and the device answers with 'Track %d has invalid plug, can't play note'. opzfix.py now applies DRUM_MASKS {13:1, 14:2, 15:4, 17:8}.

hypothesis: The app's 'chorus-80 on the kick' is a DLC-catalogue id collision, not a different track numbering
test: Read PlugManager::_importSlotConfiguration's hard-coded default map and the catalogue's own plug 13
notes: The decompiled app hard-codes the fallback slot map 'slot 0..15 = 13, 14, 15, 17, 21, 25, 28, 31, 34, 36, 37, 39, 60, 70, 80, 100' used whenever settings/slotConfiguration.json is unreadable, and the 0-byte ~NN.engine markers in the sample packs are an export of that map, so slot 0 (the kick) really is plug id 13. TE's DLC catalogue gives id 13 the name chorus-80 and engine chorus2.engine at trackmask 768, which is a tracks 9-10 FX plug. The app displays plug names by looking up its own catalogue by id, so a device plug with id 13 shows as chorus-80 whatever engine it holds - and the same collision is what puts chorus2.engine on the kick track and produces the null-function crash.

hypothesis: A drum sample pack installs as its own plug (150-153 for the redmount pack), not on plug 13
test: Read the catalogue's sampler plug records and reproduce the app's shape host-side
notes: Catalogue sampler plugs: 121-124 te-kicks/snares/perc/fx, 130-133 z-*, 134-137 cuckoo *, 140-143 seba *, 150-153 rdmt kicks/snares/perc/fx, all engine sampleplayergain with per-track samples .aif names and masks 1/2/4/8. So the app installs a pack by creating such a plug and re-pointing the drum track at it through slotConfiguration.json, which is why nothing placed on the fixed ids 13/14/15/17 ever produced a drum sample. The payload now defines 150-153 with samples redmountKicks/Snares/Perc/FX.aif, sets tracks 0-3 to those plugs, and writes the four .aif files to both ../user/samplepacks/<name>.aif and ../user/samplepacks/user/<name>.aif.

hypothesis: Sample packs can be added through the content disk at any free slot folder under the track directory
test: Read how_to_import.txt's sample-pack section and its ADD/MODIFY/REMOVE table
notes: The device's own manual lists sample packs as add/modify/remove = yes/no/yes, states the supported format is the OP-1 .aif sample format (drum format for drum tracks, synth format for synth tracks), and says 'the 10 slots of a track is represented by ten sub folders under each track. choose a free slot folder and place your new sample pack there', naming 1-kick/01/<pack>.aif as the example. This supersedes the earlier reading that samples are not a content-disk import type: the import's 'Calculating used sample space' step measures the dropped packs.

hypothesis: The 0-byte ~-prefixed files in the samplepacks tree are duplicate markers, not engine requests
test: Read how_to_import.txt's duplicate explanation and list every non-zero file in the tree
notes: how_to_import.txt: 'only one sample pack per slot folder will be imported, any additional ones will be rejected. you can place the same sample pack on several tracks without taking up any redundant diskspace. the duplicate files will be prefixed with ~ and have 0 size', with a worked example. Listing the disk confirmed no non-zero file exists anywhere under samplepacks/ - only the eight 0-byte duplicates (1-kick/01/~121.engine, the redmount ~ .aif markers in 2-snare/3-perc/4-fx/01, and 5-bass/6-lead/7-arpeggio/8-chord/01/~21,25,28,31.engine) - so no drum track held any audio and import.log read 0.0/24.0 MB on all four import runs.

hypothesis: The content-disk eject sync strips /yaffs2/user/engines/
test: Compare the synth-engine init time and the 'Can't load engine' lines before and after the content-mode eject
notes: After the eject that installed the sample packs, the boot logged 'main: initialize [synth engine]: took 133523 ms' - 133 seconds, one failed load timeout per plug - with 'instrumentmanag: Can't load engine 14/17/...' for every plug whose engine is a file. Before that eject the same boot took 53 ms with no load failures. So engine binaries written through the updater do not survive a content-disk eject and must be re-staged after one.

hypothesis: The stale 1-kick/01/~121.engine duplicate marker is what makes PLAY crash
test: Read the rebuild's engine request for that marker and define plug 121 explicitly in plugs.json
notes: how_to_import.txt says a ~-prefixed 0-byte file is a duplicate marker for a pack of that name in another slot folder, so '~121.engine' asks for a pack file named 121.engine that was never delivered. The boot logs 'instrumentmanag: Can't load engine 121', leaving plug 121 with a null sample object - and PLAY's fault is exactly a null sample object read (iid 0x00130026, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0, RETX 0x80117baa). Payload now defines plug 121 (engine engines/sampleplayergain.engine, samples redmountKicks.aif, trackmask 1) so the id resolves to a pack that exists; if PLAY still faults, the markers themselves get deleted through the content disk, which supports REMOVE.

hypothesis: A plug whose pack cannot resolve leaves the null sample object that PLAY dereferences
test: Track which plugs have unresolvable samples when PLAY faults
notes: Every observed PLAY fault is iid 0x00130026 / ADI_EXC_DATA_CPLB_MISS / DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0 / RETX 0x80117baa, a load at offset 0x2c0 from a null base, i.e. a field read on the sample object. It appeared while the drum tracks were silent, persisted while engine 121 could not load, and the same log shows the fx manager asking for a plug id (109) that plugs.json did not define. Defining every requested id against a pack that exists is what removes the null.

hypothesis: Overwriting settings/plugs.json with sampler plugs destroys the device's rebuilt pack plugs and the sound
test: Correlate the lost sound with the payload that replaced plugs.json, and the flood with its samples values
notes: The device's own 'Rebuilding plug definitions' step builds the working pack plugs from the content disk and persists them to settings/plugs.json. The payload staged afterwards rewrote that file with 25 plugs, including eight sampler plugs (121-124 and 150-153) whose samples names (redmountKicks/Snares/Perc/FX.aif) no longer resolve, because the copies at samplepacks/user/ had been garbage-collected as unused at the previous boot and the packs that play live in the device's own store. The drum tracks then lost the plugs they resolve through (silence) and the eight unresolvable plugs supplied the null sample object PLAY faults on.

hypothesis: An unresolvable samples value causes an infinite retry loop that destroys the crash record
test: Count the alternating ENOENT and AIFF_ReadOpen pairs in the newest crash log
notes: The newest crash record (device time 21:44:20) consists of 62 identical 'yaffsfs: yaffs: error: ENOENT' plus 'libaiff: AIFF_ReadOpen failed: failed to open' pairs and contains no iid, RETX or FAULT_ADDR lines at all, because the 7,152-byte record is a rolling tail the flood overwrote. The payload staged afterwards therefore contains no sampler plug, so that no samples value can be unresolvable.

hypothesis: Sample packs register from a content-disk slot folder, and duplicates are deduplicated by assignment
test: Read the import log's per-pack lines
notes: The import log shows 'importing redmountKicks.aif...SUCCESS. New used space 870 kB' for the newly delivered kick pack (891,612 bytes becoming 870 kB of registered sample memory), and 'assigning snare/02/redmountSnares.aif', 'assigning perc/02/redmountPerc.aif', 'assigning fx/02/redmountFX.aif' for the three packs the device already held, which cost no additional space. So the content disk is the working ingress for sample audio, and 'Rebuilding plug definitions...SUCCESS' that follows derives the drum plugs from the marker tree itself.

hypothesis: The kick pack's device id is not reconstructible from the host
test: Compare the ~-239494487 marker against crc32/adler32/md5/sha1 of the pack's name, path and content
notes: The marker naming the imported kick pack is '~-239494487' while the assigned packs got catalogue ids 151/152/153 (rdmt snares/perc/fx), because those were already known to the device and the kick pack was new. crc32 of the file name, of the content bytes (1381011654), of several path spellings, adler32 of the content, and truncated md5/sha1 all fail to produce -239494487 (unsigned 4055472809, hex f1b99aa9). Since the host cannot compute the ids the device puts in its own plug table, settings/plugs.json must not be written from the host at all.

hypothesis: The app's sample uploads abort on a stale engine crc check before the apply phase that promotes the inbox file
test: Read the app-session log's per-item sequence
notes: Every item follows the same sequence: the sample transfers fine ('Download complete: [/yaffs2/user/inbox/samplepacks/redmountSnares.aif]', 'file complete. crc: 1a0ea97 == 1a0ea97?'), then the engine step is skipped as already matching ('Ignore File request engines/sampleplayergain.engine, same crc: 26d66594'), then the job aborts with 'invalid file crc, can't finalize /yaffs2/user/engines/sampleplayergain.engine (0 != 26d66594)' because the skipped file was never written and reads as crc 0. The apply phase that moves inbox/<path> into place never runs, so the audio stays in /yaffs2/user/inbox/ and the plug is imported anyway ('plugmanager: found plug to import, id:151 index:0'), leaving a slot claim with no audio behind it.

hypothesis: The app is reliable for engines and plug selection but its sample audio stops in the inbox
test: Compare every registration attempt against the import log's used-sample-space counter
notes: Writing packs into /yaffs2/user/ by any other route - flat at the root, under samplepacks/, under samplepacks/user/, or in the slot folders, all through the updater - produced a retry flood, a 'Remove unused sample pack' garbage collection, or silence, and never an entry in 'Calculating used sample memory'. The only registration ever observed is the content-disk import ('importing redmountKicks.aif...SUCCESS. New used space 870 kB'), and the app's own plugs do get created ('plugmanager: found plug to import, id:151 index:0').

hypothesis: The app's bindings leave plugs whose packs have no audio, and those are what PLAY faults on
test: Compare the surviving kick slot 01 with the app-created slots and the boot's engine-load errors
notes: The crash is unchanged (iid 0x00130026, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0, RETX 0x80117baa) while the disk-installed kick pack still plays and the boot still reports it (used sample memory 870 kB). The log names every app-created binding by id as an engine it cannot load: 121 te-kicks, 122 te-snares, 130 z-kicks, 134 cuckoo kicks, 140/141 seba, 151/152/153 rdmt and the imported pack's private -239494487. A ~<plugid>.engine marker makes the device treat that id as having a file-based engine named <plugid>.engine, which does not exist, and a plug whose pack has no audio leaves the null sample object PLAY dereferences. The redmount bindings survive because their packs were imported through the content disk.

hypothesis: Deleting the audio-less markers through the content disk clears both the engine-load errors and the PLAY fault
test: Remove the ~<plugid>.engine markers with no audio, eject, and check the rebuild
notes: Sample packs support REMOVE on the content disk, and the eject's 'Rebuilding plug definitions' step drops the plugs those markers created and re-derives the slot map. Keeping only the bindings whose audio exists (151, 152, 153, -239494487 and the ~redmount*.aif markers) should leave no plug without samples, which is the only observed source of the null sample object at DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0. The updater cannot do this, since it only writes and never deletes.

hypothesis: Deleting a ~ marker from the content disk does not remove the device's binding for that pack
test: Delete the two remaining audio-less markers, eject, and compare the next boot's engine-load errors
notes: After deleting 1-kick/02/~134.engine and 2-snare/02/~141.engine the next boot still logged 'Can't load engine 134' and 'Can't load engine 141', and PLAY still faulted with iid 0x00130026 / DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x000002c0 / RETX 0x80117baa. A ~ file is a duplicate marker, i.e. a reference to a pack whose real entry lives elsewhere, so removing the reference leaves the device's own binding and its missing audio intact.

hypothesis: Giving a slot real audio re-derives its binding, and that is the way to replace an audio-less binding
test: Put redmountKicks.aif into 1-kick/02 and redmountSnares.aif into 2-snare/02, eject, and test PLAY
notes: The kick's working slot 01 carries a real redmountKicks.aif and its binding was derived from that audio (the device assigned it the private id -239494487), while every app binding is a ~<plugid>.engine reference with no audio. So putting real packs into the slots that held plugs 134 and 141 should replace those bindings with audio-backed ones, leaving no plug without samples - the only observed source of the null sample object PLAY dereferences.

hypothesis: PLAY's crash is triggered by the FX manager failing to find plug 109, in the same second
test: Read the lines immediately preceding the exception in the newest crash record
notes: The crash record ends with '[22:15:34] fxmanager: Couldn't find plug with id 109' immediately followed by '[22:15:34] main: exception caught iid: 0x00130026', 'exc reason: ADI_EXC_DATA_CPLB_MISS', 'DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR: 0x000002c0', 'callstack: RETX: 0x80117baa'. The same message appears three times at boot (harmless) and a fourth time at PLAY, where it is followed by the fault in the same second. The app's catalogue gives plug 109 the name crush, engine crush.engine and trackmask 768, i.e. the two FX tracks, and its table defines it ('plugmanager: found plug to import, id:109 index:22') while the device's own marker-derived rebuild does not, since no marker names 109.

hypothesis: Replacing a slot's ~ reference with real audio removes the audio-less plug, as it did for 134
test: Put a real redmountSnares.aif into 2-snare/01 and check that 'Can't load engine 141' stops
notes: After 1-kick/02 was given a real redmountKicks.aif, the following boot logged no 'Can't load engine 134' at all, whereas 134 had failed four times in the boot before. The same slot still carried the cuckoo-kicks binding before the replacement. 2-snare/01 still holds only '~redmountSnares.aif' and still produces 'Can't load engine 141' three times per boot, so giving it real audio should clear it the same way.

hypothesis: A ~<plugid>.engine marker is the host-side way to make the device's rebuild define a plug
test: Create samplepacks/9-fx/01/~109.engine and check whether the fx manager stops reporting it missing
notes: The device's rebuild derives its whole plug table from the samplepack markers: that is how plugs 121, 122, 130, 134, 140, 141, 151, 152 and 153 came into existence as '~<plugid>.engine' files written by the app's installs. Plug 109 (catalogue: crush, engine crush.engine, trackmask 768, the two FX tracks) is defined by the app's own table ('plugmanager: found plug to import, id:109 index:22') but not by the rebuild, and the crash follows 'fxmanager: Couldn't find plug with id 109' by zero seconds. A marker should therefore define it without overwriting settings/plugs.json.

hypothesis: PLAY crashes because nine of the ten project slots are empty and the sequencer runs against the active project
test: Fill projects/project01..08,10.opz from the device's own exported project09.opz, eject, and test PLAY
notes: Every boot logs 'serialize: Failed to load project /yaffs2/user/projects/projectNN.opz' for 01-08 and 10, while project09 never appears in that list, so exactly one slot exists. The PLAY fault carries the sequencer's voice-allocation callstack (0x8002c438, 0x11a03838, 0x11a02586, 0x11a0203c, 0x80133c78, 0x80112b06, 0x80134a04) and arrives with nothing logged before it - on the newest boot 49 seconds after the last line - so no plug, sample or engine message is the trigger. Projects are an ADD-able content type on the content disk, named project01.opz to project10.opz, and a genuine 342,848-byte project09.opz exported from this device is on the host.

hypothesis: A ~<plugid>.engine marker only defines a plug when it sits in a real track folder
test: Place ~109.engine under a new 9-fx/01 directory and check whether plug 109 appears
notes: The marker left in samplepacks/9-fx/01/~109.engine did not create plug 109: the following boot still logs 'fxmanager: Couldn't find plug with id 109' three times. The markers that did create plugs (121, 122, 130, 134, 140, 141, 151, 152, 153) all sat in the device's own track directories 1-kick through 8-chord, whose names follow the <n>-<name> pattern the disk's track folders use, so an unrecognised folder is apparently ignored.

hypothesis: A ~109.engine marker in a real track directory creates plug 109; in an unrecognised folder it does not
test: Place the marker under samplepacks/8-chord/02 and check whether the three-miss block stops
notes: The first attempt used samplepacks/9-fx/01/~109.engine and the following boot still logged 'fxmanager: Couldn't find plug with id 109' three times at initialisation and three more times immediately before the PLAY fault. Every marker that ever created a plug (121, 122, 130, 134, 140, 141, 151, 152, 153) sat inside one of the device's own track directories 1-kick to 8-chord, whose names follow the <n>-<name> pattern, so a newly invented folder is apparently ignored. Plug 109's catalogue mask is 768, the two FX tracks, which cannot legitimately bind to a drum or synth track, so the marker's purpose is only to make the plug exist for the FX manager's lookup.

hypothesis: This unit has never held a valid project, and PLAY runs against that invalid project
test: Inspect the project09.opz we were copying and read the loader's rejection of it
notes: project09.opz (342,848 bytes, 0x53b40) is an all-zero stub: the first 96 bytes are zeros, entropy is 0.52 bits/byte, there is no zlib or zip header, no ASCII, and only 88 distinct byte values. Once the file was actually delivered (through the updater, which produced a different error), the loader reported 'serialize: Failed to load GlobalData from /yaffs2/user/projects/project01.opz, wrong format: 0' - it reads a format field, gets 0, and gives up. The internal user filesystem was formatted when the NAND was wiped and no project has existed since, which is consistent with PLAY failing from the very first boot.

hypothesis: Only the device (or the app) can write a valid project file
test: Have the device save a project, then check whether the boot's project errors clear
notes: The project container has a format field the loader validates and the export we held was never initialised, so a valid file cannot be synthesised from the host side. Both the device (its own project save) and the app (which exposes loadProject/saveProject/saveProjectAs/convertProject) write that format. The updater proved it can deliver a file to exactly the right place, so once one valid project exists it can be copied into the remaining slots.

hypothesis: The content disk imports sample audio but does not import projects from the host
test: Compare the sample-memory jump after a disk restore with the unchanged project load failures
notes: After restoring the healthy backup's contents onto the disk, the next boot's 'Calculating used sample memory' rose from 870 kB to 1567 kB - almost exactly the 183,660 + 529,696 bytes of the two restored user samples - so sample audio imports. The same boot still logged all nine 'Failed to load GlobalData from /yaffs2/user/projects/projectNN.opz, wrong format: 0' errors, i.e. it was still reading the zero-filled stubs written earlier through the updater and the disk's 'Syncronizing projects' step had replaced nothing. Projects must therefore travel through the updater.

hypothesis: The restored 351 KB userPresets.dat is what moved the crash from PLAY to initialisation
test: Write a zero-filled bank of the same size through the updater and check whether the boot completes
notes: Before the backup restore the device booted and only PLAY faulted; afterwards the fault occurs in initialisation, immediately after 'snakesystem: load general config /yaffs2/user/config/general.json', with a new fault address 0x00000000 (previously 0x000002c0) and new callstack frames 0x8011a0c0 and 0x8011a184. The next step in that sequence is the presets load, and config/userPresets.dat (351,202 bytes) is the only restored file that is both a large binary and parsed at that point. The repair writes a zero-filled file of the same size, the empty 200-record state the device writes itself.

hypothesis: A zero-filled userPresets.dat crashes the boot; the file must carry format field 1 or be absent
test: Read 'plugmanager: Wrong file format' and compare the backup's file header with the zeroed one
notes: The boot crash appeared only after the preset bank was replaced, and the log names it: 'plugmanager: Wrong file format: /yaffs2/user/config/userPresets.dat (0 != 1)' immediately followed by the fault (iid 0x00130026, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, RETX 0x80117baa). The healthy file is 351,202 bytes with format field 1 in its first bytes and 200 x 1,756 bytes of records; a zero-filled file of the same size reads as format 0 and is rejected. When the file was simply absent the device logged a harmless ENOENT and booted, so only the genuine file or no file at all is acceptable.

hypothesis: Only a staged-and-verified payload can be assumed to have landed
test: Compare opzfix.py's console-captured extract counter against a raw copy and eject
notes: Staging through opzfix.py produced '[extract] progress 3873439/3873439' in the captured console and zero 'Failed to extract' lines, whereas the earlier raw cp plus diskutil eject of a 3,874,458-byte archive produced no extract progress lines in the device log at all, leaving it unknown whether that payload was applied. Waiting for the progress counter to reach its total is the only confirmed signal.

hypothesis: A missing engines/tapetwo.engine crashes both boot modes in the plug manager's initialisation
test: Compare the shared crash signature with the unconditional TapeTwo initialisation and the staged engine set
notes: All five crash records are identical (iid 0x00130026, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, RETX 0x80117baa, callstack 8002c438 11a03838 11a02586 08003e0c) and occur at the plug manager's initialisation, in normal and content mode alike, because that step is shared. The decompiled app shows PlugManager::init always inserts crc32('engines/tapetwo.engine') and calls TapeTwo::initModule unconditionally, unlike loadRequestedEngines which returns on an empty list, so a missing tapetwo binary nulls that call. The content-disk eject strips /yaffs2/user/engines/ every pass and the payload staged to fix the markers contained only the thirteen numbered engine copies, not the twenty-one real-name binaries, so tapetwo.engine was absent.

hypothesis: A firmware reinstall rewrites the content component and is the recovery path from an unreadable poisoned user state
test: Stage z_firmware_1_2_45.zfw and read the upgrade console lines
notes: The installer reported '[extract] progress 2775623/2775623', '[content] progress 18/18', 'copied 18 files', 'content: OK (0)', 'os: OK (0)' and 'successfully upgraded to 1.2.45'. Unlike updater writes, which can only add files, the install re-copies the firmware's content component and can therefore replace state that is neither readable nor deletable from the host, such as settings/plugs.json and the samplepack marker tree. It does not use the console type 0x15 NAND format that bricked the unit originally.

hypothesis: A firmware reinstall rewrites the internal user content to the factory default set
test: List the content disk's samplepacks tree after the 1.2.45 reinstall
notes: After the reinstall the disk's samplepacks tree contains only the factory default markers - ~13/~14/~15/~17 on the four drum tracks, ~21/~25/~28/~31 as each synth track's first engine marker, and a ~10/~14/~17 spread - with no redmount packs, no .aif files, no projects/ directory, and a config/ reduced to dmx.json and general.json. Every file written before the install (78+109 markers, sample audio, ten projects, the backup config, two user samples) was gone, and content mode began working immediately afterwards. This corrects the earlier note that an install does not wipe the user tree, which only covered one specific observation.

hypothesis: The boot fault is in the plug-to-sample binding after loadSettings and disappears when any real sample pack resolves
test: Reconstruct lib_init's order from the app binary, bracket the fault with the device's own log lines, and tabulate used sample memory against boot outcome
notes: lib_init is preInit -> loadSettings -> saveSettings -> SynthInit (InstrumentManager::init then FxManager::init) -> sequencerInit -> MidiInit, and loadSettings logs 'load general config %s' before it tests existence, so a crash immediately after that line is in saveSettings or Synth::init; the missing-file boot crashes identically, which rules the JSON parse out, and the boots that work all show the failed open of /yaffs2/system/content/samplepacks/sfx.aif, which the crashing boots never reach. Failed engine loads are tolerated (five 'dlm: Bad address' failures on 2026-10-10 20:00 still reached the sequencer), the fault is invariant with and without plugs.json, and readPlugSettings reads only flags/version/engine/samples per plug, so a host table carrying those keys is parsed. Every booting state had a non-zero 'Calculating used sample memory' (88 kB, 870 kB, 3594 kB) and every crashing state had 0 kB, including the post-0x15-format one where the internal packs are 0-byte; both crash classes share RETX 0x80117baa, only the faulting address differs (0x000002c0 at PLAY, 0x00000000 at boot).

hypothesis: Real .aif packs placed in free drum-track slots restore the boot
test: Content mode: copy the four redmount packs into samplepacks/{1-kick,2-snare,3-perc,4-fx}/02, eject, re-stage the engines with ENGINES_ONLY=True, then power on normally
notes: The content disk is the only route that has ever delivered audible sample audio (it made all four drum tracks sound on 2026-10-10 22:38) and it is the mechanism that re-derives a track's plug from the audio itself; the eject strips /yaffs2/user/engines/ and runs 'Rebuilding plug definitions', so the engines are re-staged afterwards through the updater while settings/plugs.json and settings/slotConfiguration.json are left to the device.

hypothesis: The boot fault needs at least one resolvable sample pack (the 0 kB/3594 kB correlation)
test: Import the four redmount packs through the content disk, re-stage the engines, then boot
notes: The import registered all four packs (importing ... SUCCESS, New used space 3594 kB, Rebuilding plug definitions SUCCESS) and the next boot still faulted at the same instruction (iid 0x00130026, ADI_EXC_DATA_CPLB_MISS, DCPLB_FAULT_ADDR 0x00000000, RETX 0x80117baa) with no sample opened, so used sample memory was a proxy for the rest of what the factory reset removed rather than the trigger itself.

hypothesis: The missing piece is the per-plug preset bank the content component does not carry (config/userPresets.dat, 200 x 1756 B, format field 1)
test: Stage the pre-brick backup's config/userPresets.dat, midi.json, general.json and the ten genuine projects plus the 21 engines through the updater, then boot normally
notes: The plug-to-voice binding in Synth::init is what the fault sits in, per-plug preset/parameter data is what it consumes, and the healthy unit's backup carries exactly one substantive file the factory state lacks: a 351,202-byte config/userPresets.dat with format field 1 (200 records x 1756 bytes). The updater writes /yaffs2/user/config/ directly and the content import additionally lists 'importing config/userPresets.dat...SUCCESS', so the file is deliverable by two independent routes.

hypothesis: The normal-boot fix is the engine files written into /yaffs2/user/samplepacks/user/<plugid>.engine plus disable_start_sound
test: Re-apply the §66.26 payload (config first, 21 numbered engines in samplepacks/user/, engines/ real+numbered, plug table, factory slot map) and boot normally
notes: §66.26 records that exactly this write moved the unit from 'dies during init' to 'startup animation, track selection, TRACK responds' on 2026-10-08. The scan that decides whether an engine exists reads the samplepacks tree, so engines placed only in /yaffs2/user/engines/ or only in track slots never satisfy it; the reinstall rewrites the content component and silently undoes the write, which is why normal mode broke again tonight.

conclusion: disproved as an APK-based causal inference
notes: The pathname is hashed as a registry key; callback slots 0x1d5600/608/610/618 resolve to linked TapeTwo init/renderFX/onNoteOn/onNoteOff. initModule is called at 0xd6ea4 without opening the pathname in this routine. This corrects §66.62's causal argument, not independent observations of missing device engines. APK/firmware equivalence remains unverified.

hypothesis: Playback step-component registration requires definitions from a missing persistent file
test: Trace StepComponentManager::init 0x105674, registerComponents 0x1047d4, reset 0x105624 and enterStep 0x106178; resolve global references
notes: Eleven linked globals are registered; reset clears state and dispatches registered callbacks, and enterStep uses pattern settings. Registration does not load NAND component definitions. Callback bodies were not exhaustively audited and no physical-device fault cause was identified. See §66.77.

hypothesis: Hashing a project pathname automatically selects its reserved FileSync read ID
test: Inspect calcFileId 0x117c58 against getFilePath 0x1179e0
notes: calcFileId performs ASCII lowercase plus CRC32 without project special cases. IDs 3-12 are explicit read aliases in getFilePath; generic hashed-path requests do not select them. The reserved-ID backup candidate remains untested on the device. No arbitrary system read or full-recovery route was established. See §66.77.

hypothesis: The existing iOS 1.3.1 app supplies the audio implementations stubbed in the Android library
test: Inspect the archived IPA's ARM64 UnityFramework symbols and exact instruction ranges after Kuna inventory exceeded a 90-second budget
conclusion: disproved for the six inspected symbols
notes: Info.plist version 1.3.1 build 194; framework SHA256 f5ddfa272688b31c07b9654dbc4aa5d8b8bc3cf8f4b0e84c99683eb79bba9c90; cryptid=0. updateRequestedSamplePacks 0x10a9a50, updateMetronome 0x10a9a54, InstrumentManager::init 0x110485c, noteOn 0x11049a8, noteOff 0x11049ac and FxManager::init 0x1110c7c are literal ret. No full-framework decompilation, app execution, new download or device action. See §66.77.

hypothesis: The inactive-sync ID gate and reserved project aliases are peculiar to the Android build
test: Cross-check iOS FileSync::handleMessage 0x109b8d4 and getFilePath 0x109bed4 with bounded disassembly and mapped string bytes
notes: iOS also rejects IDs >=100 when inactive. Its lookup subtracts two for IDs 3-12, formats projects/project%02d.opz, and uses a tree for higher IDs. This corroborates the read-only project-backup candidate without proving device behavior. No literal sfx.aif string was found in the framework; that is not an exhaustive asset search or a device-file existence test. See §66.77.

hypothesis: The genuine engine files expose recoverable native entry points for a diagnostic-module feasibility study
test: Walk engines-official/crush.engine loader records and resolve its name/address table through mapped blocks
notes: Crush is 1012 B, SHA256 f1542de16fddca835c6becdb0d809f7e16d75c5e7c19bde2da31c1dca6da34f9. The table begins feed0ad1/ad1facef and resolves initModule 0x81bfb450, init 0x81bfb4bc, renderFX 0x81bfb4f0, onNoteOn 0x81bfb444 and onNoteOff 0x81bfb438. This identifies locations, not acceptance of modified code or a working memory reader. No engine modified or executed. See §66.78.

hypothesis: Consistent engine loader headers prove modified payloads will be accepted without authentication
test: Walk all 21 official streams and check header bytes; distinguish container evidence from unknown firmware-loader policy
notes: All 138 sixteen-byte headers have upper code byte ad and bytewise XOR zero; every stream ends exactly at EOF. These properties do not prove absence of payload authentication or acceptance of modifications. Firmware loader code is unavailable; no modified-module test was performed. See §66.78.

hypothesis: A diagnostic engine has an established channel for returning arbitrary device memory
test: Inspect native exports and APK Crush::initModule 0x123460, renderFX 0x1234a4 and callback-table ELF relocations
notes: Native renderFX export plus APK audio-buffer writes support audio as a candidate channel. The inspected APK callback table exposes sequencer/DSP/preset helpers, not an established general log/MIDI/file-output API. Native ABI, OS-memory permissions and byte-exact output remain unverified. Kuna rejects raw engine format; radare2 6.2.2 command `r2 -q -a bfin -b 16 -c 'i;pd 8' engines-official/crush.engine` reports `asm.arch: cannot find 'bfin'`, then prints raw bytes, not instructions. `rasm2 -L` also lists no Blackfin plugin; no `bfin-elf-objdump` was available. Native bodies remain undisassembled. See §66.78.

hypothesis: The existing file writer and a saved original engine make a diagnostic-engine trial safely reversible
test: Assess acceptance, native ABI, output and boot-independent rollback prerequisites without touching the device
notes: File placement and a host backup do not prove recovery from an engine that breaks boot. No verified rollback or safely isolated activation exists for this proposal. Do not replace Crush, TapeTwo or other engines yet. Next offline milestone is native Blackfin disassembly of the genuine exports; no device commands, modifications, installation or execution occurred. See §66.78.

hypothesis: A BF703 engine can be reliably pseudodecompiled using an available host toolchain
test: Build BF70x-capable bfin-elf-objdump, extract Crush loader payload blocks, disassemble at mapped destinations and inspect generated instructions and unsupported words
notes: Built deanm1278/blackfin-plus-gnu revision e4408a15b9be6cd911283f103a1a3f69e9a6b8c0 objdump locally; exported Crush onNoteOff/onNoteOn decode as LINK/UNLINK/RTS/NOP and init/renderFX yield partial Blackfin+ assembly. Fork documents incomplete BF70x support and emits ILLEGAL at code addresses 0x81bfb454/468/5c4/602, so this is not verified full disassembly or C pseudocode. Ghidra Blackfin+ extension source is untested; Kuna slacomp rejects its spec; full Ghidra (~570 MB) is not installed. No device activity or engine modification. See §66.79.

hypothesis: Ghidra 12.1.4 and a Blackfin+ extension can import and pseudodecompile genuine OP-Z engine exports
test: Install Ghidra/native macOS decompiler, compile the Blackfin+ SLEIGH spec, import Crush via its boot-stream loader, seed export functions, and run Ghidra DecompInterface
notes: Ghidra 12.1.4 installed at ~/Applications/Ghidra_12.1.4; mac_arm_64 decompiler built successfully. HEKAR extension source revision 380b86f1de8c69e3ce433f93a93cb771fc90d3dc required a small Ghidra 12.1.4 loader API adaptation and is explicitly untested; SLEIGH compiled with 72 NOP and 20 local-operand warnings. Import mapped all four initialized blocks. Ghidra decompiled five exports: note handlers return; initModule/init/renderFX produce plausible but unvalidated C. Incorrect inferred type on init and BF+ extension limits remain. Engine unmodified/unexecuted; no device access. See §66.80.

hypothesis: Static review of the 21 official engine exports exposes a firmware-memory read/output primitive
test: Import all genuine engine modules into the experimental BF+ Ghidra extension, decompile five exported functions each, and trace direct memory/callback access
notes: Revalidated all 21 loader streams, header XORs, export-table sentinels; tables each expose initModule, init, onNoteOn, onNoteOff, render/renderFX. Ghidra pseudocode succeeded for 104/105 exports; fdnreverb.renderFX timed out at 60s and 300s. initModule generally stores a host callback-table pointer and requests bounded memory; several exports call indirect host callbacks, but actual BF703 callback meanings are unknown. Decompiled static globals all fell within each engine's mapped payload; no direct memory/file/console primitive was established. Pointer arguments and incomplete/untested SLEIGH semantics prevent a negative proof. No engine modification/execution or device access. See §66.81.

hypothesis: The inspected Android callback table lets an engine request arbitrary filesystem paths
test: Decompile APK getPresetData and FileManager::readFile, then check the callback table relocations
notes: In OP-Z_1.3.0_APKPure.apk, getPresetData selects fixed rendertone.preset or engines/fmedit.preset paths and calls FileManager::readFile with a 0x1000-byte limit; this callback does not accept an engine-supplied path. This says nothing conclusive about other tables or the physical firmware. See §66.82.

hypothesis: The Android callback table provides a verified mapping for BF703 engine callbacks
test: Cross-check the APK callback relocations and call signatures against genuine engine indirect-call offsets
notes: In the inspected APK, TapeTwo uses interface +8 with argument 4 for sequencerGetValue, while the genuine BF+ TapeTwo engine uses +4 with 4; engine calls at +0x1c/+0x20 have five/seven arguments matching APK updateParametersADSR/updateParametersAHD. This supports ABI hypotheses only. The engine +0x24 callback and physical firmware table remain unresolved; APK/device equivalence is unverified. See §66.82.

hypothesis: Early OP-1 Field firmware provides an independent offline copy of the OP-Z AES key
test: Check public OP-1 Field firmware repositories and the researcher's published decryption notes
notes: An OP-Forums researcher reports the OP-Z key was also used by early OP-1 Field firmware and explains it was found by scanning the already-decrypted OP-Z bootloader. The public OP-1 Field archive lists .tfw ciphertext releases only; no key or decrypted bootloader was published in the inspected sources. This cross-product lead does not itself yield plaintext. See §66.83; https://op-forums.com/t/custom-firmware-on-the-op-1/4283?page=44

hypothesis: Decrypting the OP-Z bootloader/key requires reading the full 466,903-byte opz.ldr OS stream
test: Walk local ZIP headers to identify the distinct bootloader member
notes: The oracle identified `firmware/blackfin/bin/bootloader.ldr` at payload offset 467,507, with 156,306 compressed and 257,644 uncompressed bytes (CRC-32 0x5087bc54). Its data starts at 467,573; only the first 106 compressed bytes are recovered. Full bootloader recovery is still open, but does not require the separate 466,903-byte opz.ldr OS stream. See §66.87.

hypothesis: The first archive entry after opz.ldr is the bootloader image
test: Walk local ZIP headers and identify the first entry
notes: The entry at 467,280 is `firmware/blackfin/bin/bootloader.version`; the actual `firmware/blackfin/bin/bootloader.ldr` entry starts at 467,507 after `opz.crc32` and `os.version`. See §66.87.

hypothesis: The ZIP member following bootloader.version is the bootloader image
test: Walk subsequent local headers and identify member names
notes: The next entries are `firmware/blackfin/bin/opz.crc32` at 467,361 and `firmware/blackfin/bin/os.version` at 467,434; the actual `firmware/blackfin/bin/bootloader.ldr` starts at 467,507. See §66.87.

hypothesis: The CCES Loader and Utilities manual narrows the OP-Z AES key to a fixed bootloader.ldr block or offset
test: Compare official BF7xx .ldr/security documentation with the OP-Z bootloader artifact
notes: The manual describes `.ldr` as code/data boot blocks and says block tags include load information (p. 2-10); BF7xx-specific details defer to the Blackfin+ Processor Hardware Reference (pp. 6-2, 6-4). Its documented secure-boot encryption is AES-128 with OTP/wrapped key options (pp. 6-3, 13-11–13), not evidence about the OP-Z updater's reported AES-256 key. It supplies no fixed key location; see §66.88.

hypothesis: The bootloader.ldr begins with a standard BF70x block header or secure-boot wrapper
test: Inflate its prefix; test the 180-byte secure-header type and 16-byte LDR header signatures/checksum
conclusion: proved: standard LDR header at offset 0
notes: The current partial stream has 811 compressed/1,211 inflated bytes (DEFLATE eof=false), beginning with three valid 16-byte BF70x LDR headers at inflated offsets 0, 16, and 124; each has the 0xAD signature and valid XOR header checksum. No 180-byte secure-boot header precedes them. The third block has only 1,071 of its 4,112 payload bytes. See §§66.90–66.92.

hypothesis: The collector stalls when a masked first-block byte equals the XOR delta
test: Reproduce a C-string terminator at relative offset 6, inspect the overlapping prior read, repair its plaintext value, and retry with another delta
notes: Seven retries at payload offset 467,808 returned the same six bytes. An earlier overlapping read established that the next byte was 0x01; delta 1 changed it to NUL, and the collector both inferred zero instead of delta and aligned back to the same window. The reader now maps first-16-byte terminators to the mask delta, repairs legacy state from recorded reads, and avoids previously used/known-byte deltas. Follow-up device cycles with masks 0x02 and 0x01 added 48 then 1 bytes, completing the 512-byte requested range; automatic volume polling also worked. Self-test passes; see §66.90.

hypothesis: The remaining bootloader.ldr can be oracle-recovered in about 60 hours under one-minute automated cycles
test: Extrapolate remaining compressed bytes using measured useful bytes per probe; multiply by an explicitly assumed full update/reboot/remount cycle
notes: After the latest 12-probe batch, 512 new bytes were recovered (42.7/probe); 811/156,306 compressed bytes are contiguous, leaving 155,495 or ~3,645 probes. The 12 decrypted frames arrived 4.506–5.476s after volume detection (mean 5.120s), while full capture completion averaged 20.510s because the 20s capture window continues after the leak. At an assumed 60s total cycle the projection is ~60.7h (2.5 days), excluding variability. Reboot/remount duration is not measured and the script does not automate update-mode entry. See §§66.91–66.92.

hypothesis: The AES-256 key occurs as an unmodified sliding 32-byte window in the recovered bootloader.ldr plaintext prefix
test: Search every one-byte-offset 32-byte window of the 1,211-byte inflated prefix; test AES-256-CBC against the hardware-verified first ZIP payload block using C(0x3f0) as the chaining block, then confirm any hit against the known decrypted filename prefix
notes: Tested all 1,180 raw sliding windows of the recovered prefix with AES-256-ECB block decrypt plus the correct CBC predecessor. No window produced the hardware-verified first 16 ZIP plaintext bytes or the first 16 known filename bytes. This rules out a raw contiguous key only in the first 1,211 inflated bytes; 811 compressed bytes of the 156,306-byte member are recovered and the key may occur later. Used the corrected §66.12 ZIP header, not its superseded hand-pasted predecessor. See §66.92.

hypothesis: An Arduino-controlled relay can automate the full bootloader oracle probe cycle
test: Run one captured probe through relay power-off/on, confirm OP-Z Boot and a fresh update volume without manual action, then time repeated volume-ready-to-volume-ready cycles
notes: The user reports the relay cuts OP-Z power even while USB is connected. Power restoration, automatic update-mode return, fresh-volume remount, and cycle timing have not yet been validated; 20 seconds is an assumption. No wiring or device-side relay trial was performed here. See §66.93 and PLAN_OPZ_BOOTLOADER_ORACLE_AUTOCYCLE.md.
